utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. I would like to greet the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and I hope Mr. Pusic will get well very soon. We shall resume with the cross-examination of the witness. In the meantime, the Trial Chamber will hand down a decision of a motion filed by the Prosecution on the 6th of June, 2007, on the admission of a new document relating to Witness Azra Krajsik. There have been no comments on the part of the Defence given the urgency in this matter. Does -- or do Defence counsel have any oral submissions to make. Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on behalf of the Praljak Defence we haven't had time to consult, but we have no objection. There is this one document, and I don't see that it has any specific significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, the Defence agrees to the motion filed by the Prosecution. This document will therefore be used when the witness comes to testify. Second item: The remaining time for the cross-examination today after our calculations it seems that there's an hour and 40 minutes left. That said, Ms. Nozica should continue with her cross-examination. Mr. Praljak and his counsel should take the floor. Mr. Petkovic and his counsel should also take the floor. From what I understood, Defence teams have not agreed on the way in which they should share the time. Some time has been granted to one and another. We don't quite know how things stand and how this time has been broken down. As we have the entire hearing of today until a quarter to 2.00, I think it is better to start with the last item and address the issue of re-examination. At this stage, Mr. Scott, have you already planned to put additional questions? If that is the case, how much time would you need for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. At this point I would estimate somewhere -- I hope this is an overestimate, but I would estimate somewhere between 20 and 30 minutes of redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we'll -- let's take it -- to be on the safe side, let's plan to have 30 minutes. I should like to put a question on how information was circulated inside UNPROFOR, though this won't take much time. Overall, I think we need to set aside one hour for redirect and questions put by the Bench, which would leave us with three hours for the Defence. So this is something in which we should be able to abide by. We only do this because we have a bit of extra time. Otherwise, we should always abide by the time limits which are set. We are going to have Ms. Nozica take the floor, then Mr. Praljak, I don't know; Defence counsel Ms. Alaburic and Mr. Stewart on behalf of General Petkovic. I know that Mr. Murphy also wanted to take the floor, but to me Ms. Nozica and Mr. Murphy are one and the same person so to speak. Ms. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just as you've just said, I have 30 minutes left of my time. I asked for 15 to 20 minutes for Mr. Murphy, but I might get through my questioning faster so we'll fall within that time limit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yesterday, we left off looking at document P 01970. And it was the order for Defence dated the 19th of April, 1993, so could you take a look at it again and they are going to give the binder back to you. Let's just see who the order was sent out to.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the English version on the penultimate page -- no, I'm sorry, the last page, let's see who the order was sent out to. If you look at the list, it was also sent to the 4th Corps command. There's no doubt about that; right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, let us also look at P 01962, and it's the second document in my binder.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: These are codes for the former order. So let's take a look at the second one, which says RAK-625. "When RAK-625 signal is given, launch a general attack on all places and assigned axes." You can look at the other two as well, but you have enough knowledge about military activities to answer my question. Can we say if we look at these codes or signals and the previous order as well, can we say it is in fact an order which represents preparation for attack?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am amazed by the order. As a military man, I would never issue such an order. It's very complicated, very long, and it doesn't make any timings for the things. It's a very unprofessional order, and it amazes me that you could start it on a code-name. But if they were together, the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in Zenica - I assume you do; I just want confirmation for you - that on the 29th of April, 1993, an agreement was signed between Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Halilovic in the presence of General Morillon and Jean-Pierre Thebault. So that was the departure to Zenica by Mr. Petkovic and Halilovic the following day and you spoke about that. And it's document 4D -- 2D, I'm sorry, 00470 is the document number and you'll find it somewhere in the middle of my binder. You already addressed the document but I'd just like to remind you of two points in that document. Tell me what you've found it, please.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you turn to page 2 where we see the individuals present when the agreement was signed, and I'd like to draw your attention to points 1 and 2. Point 1 because we discussed this yesterday during the cross-examination, and it is a very important point and says that: "The Bosnia-Herzegovina army and the HVO are legal military forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and are treated equally." And point 2 says the following: "Commanders at all levels or from all instances must respect and immediately enforce absolute cease-fire on the entire territory of the republic. Cease-fire violations are unacceptable regardless of the reasons. Both commanders immediately issued orders to respect the aforementioned." I'm sure your acquainted with this agreement as well. I don't know whether you've seen it before, but I'm sure you know of its contents, at least with regard to the cessation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was about the same thing that was said in Mostar before.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it has exactly the same importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What I wanted to hear was perhaps your comment. Do you know that both the military commanders, in the presence of Mr. Thebault and Mr. Morillon, agreed that the BH army and the HVO were legal military forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had never or I don't remember having read the first paragraph or seen it in this content. I did not regard them at the time when the conflict started as any of them really -- I think that the Muslim forces definitely regarded themselves as a legal part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the other part, I'm not so sure that I looked at it at that -- in that context at the moment. But I accept this paper. I haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to have a little clarification, General. On line 23, you have given a somewhat enigmatic answer by saying that it has exactly the same importance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's what you meant --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- none. Okay. Thank you. Could you -- could you perhaps specify why you say this? Because obviously for the -- I'm sorry. The Defence obviously attaches importance to it, and it's perhaps a bit -- a bit unsatisfactory if you simply say no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is due to my cynical experiences of all cease-fire agreements signed. They were most of the time signed by one or the other party to gain time, not because it was serious. There were other motives behind signing such a document. One could be to show oneself better or for the international community, but most of the time it was a question of gaining time for some other things. To prepare in this case maybe for a war that broke out a few weeks later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a follow-up question I'd like to put to you, General. I listened carefully to what you said, but the document we have before us which has been signed by General Halilovic and General Petkovic, there is also the signature of General Morillon here in addition to those two signatures, Philippe Morillon being at the head of UNPROFOR in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in addition we also have the signature of the person in charge of the European Monitoring Mission. This document is stamped "International." If you allow me to put it to you this way: Had you been in the shoes of Mr. Morillon, would you have signed this document, or would you have signed it, as you seem to say, at the time any document was being signed and perhaps that that was not so important after all? What would you have done in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is very hard to answer, because I was not in the situation not together with Ambassador Thebault or the atmosphere at the meeting. I would probably also have signed it to make an impression that the international community and the UN -- the UN were present and witnessed this signature of the two parties. So I think that is all what Morillon's signature means. He verifies that he has been present and a witness that the two parties has agreed to a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A colleague of mine would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Just let me add in paragraph 3 it says: "UNPROFOR will provide all necessary help," and that could also be a reason for Morillon to sign on this agreement, that he stands as a guarantee for the UNPROFOR that they will undertake all necessary help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that as a rule that kind of agreement was signed to gain time. I would like you to tell me in relation to item 4, the chiefs or heads will attend a -- weekly meetings in order to ensure close cooperation and so on and so forth. So did things actually happen this way so that this agreement could be implemented, or didn't it really mean anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if they met, but if so, there couldn't have been many meetings, if any, if any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I would like to pick up on what has just been said and as a follow-up question. This agreement which we have in front of us here, this is not to the consequence of a meeting between Halilovic and Petkovic and unbiased observers who come to sign the document. Right from the outset we can see that there has been a joint meeting that has been chaired by General Morillon and by Mr. Thebault. And when such a meeting is presided by people like this conclusions are drawn, and the first conclusion that comes to mind is that we acknowledge that ABiH and the HVO are the legal military forces in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and should be addressed as such, i.e., on an equal footing. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose that it depends on how the parties will interpret those lines, if they will put the stress on the word "legal forces" and be treated as such or if you would put the emphasis on "legal forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina." There may be a slight nuance in how you see this phrasing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There's another thing that is a bit puzzling, General, but maybe it is beyond your competence and then you just say so. What strikes me is that we read here that the two armies are to be treated equally, but treated equally by whom? There is no third party that would treat them equally, or is it that the international organisations should treat them equally anyhow, I suppose. They should be neutral. And there is no one that actually assumes any obligation outside those who enter this agreement unless they had credentials that they were representing their governments. Do you have any idea? Could you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your question is well-founded, and I cannot answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Nozica, I apologise for this, but it was important to look into this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General, linked to the last question by Judge Trechsel, who is it who would have had to recognise the legality of both sides? Who would be called upon to do that? Before Their Honours' questions, you said that you hadn't seen the document before and that up until then the BH army represented itself as being the sole legal army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I don't want you to speculate, but can you say that in fact by this the representative of the BH army -- or not the representative but the -- but Mr. Sefer Halilovic, the Chief of Staff, in fact, of the Supreme Command of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina de facto is recognising the HVO as the legitimate military force of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and without a doubt both of them were on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It overrides my legal capacity to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. You said that this agreement was one of a series of agreements which was signed as a matter of course but with the intention of not actually being acted on. Now, at the time that you were in Mostar, did you provide conditions for a truce when you described that night when, in a very dramatic way, you transported soldiers of the BH army from the Mostar Hotel? Were you also convinced then, as you are today, that you were just doing a job which the very next day would be violated by one or the other side, and that you were risking your life for something that was not going to be put into effect? Or did you believe at the time that it was possible to establish a cease-fire and truce and that therefore you acted accordingly?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will become a bit emotional when I answer this one. If you are met by old ladies down in the street serving you tea and cakes and asking you to save their Mostar and you have almost no resources at your hands and you see where things are going, you really have some motivation to try. And when I went to take out this Muslim unit at the Hotel Mostar, I did it because the Croats claimed that this was the obstacle for bringing their troops back to the barracks. So I think it was more to take away a negotiation obstacle that could at least make it more difficult for them not to fulfil the obligations and the orders given by both General Petkovic and Halilovic. So that was the reason why I did it. And it was my very last card to play because, as I said yesterday, I had to do something or give it up and go home to Zagreb, and I tried to do this -- I'm not certain, in hindsight, that this was a very wise moment. Probably most unnecessary; it didn't help.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General, both you and I know that these emotional reasons that you described were not the reasons why you got engaged in this action, but my question was the following: I know why you got involved in all of it. My question was: Did you believe that there was a chance at creating peace on the basis of the conditions that you described and that you tried to create?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to object to -- the role of counsel is to put questions to the witness and not to make observations or assertions, and if she says, "Both you and I know that these emotional reasons that you described were not the reasons why you got engaged," well, don't make those statements and then not put it in the form of a question that the witness can respond to. She has asserted that he's just stated the reasons that were not the real reasons, because the witness gave a very personal answer which I greatly respect saying the reasons why he did what he did. And counsel's just stood up and asserted those aren't the real reasons without giving him the opportunity to respond. That's not appropriate. So I ask the witness to be able to respond to counsel's assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Nozica, the witness did explain why he had acted that way, and you then said that these were not the right reasons. Don't ask the witness to say things which he hasn't said. If you don't agree with him, put a question to him and on what basis do you disagree with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Antonetti, I believe that I did just that. I asked the witness whether he believed that a truce could be achieved, and that was as a result of his answer that agreements were signed in order that they might be violated. However, I give up on this line of questioning. I will move on to another document that I believe is very relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is opened and it must be closed, and it might be closed by the General asking two questions. First, did you do what you did motivated by the scene with the old lady in the street or for some other reasons? And what was the other reason? And second question: Did you believe in a cease-fire materialising and working, or did you not? I think these two questions, we are entitled to an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I did it because we had an agreement by the two Supreme Commanders of the two forces, and I was there tasked to promote peace in Mostar. Then I took a big chance that night which probably I said was influenced emotionally because I ran the risk rather than giving up. But I did it, of course, with the specific intent that I thought that there was still a chance to get the cease-fire to hold, and I had -- I simply had to try this thing. It has to do with self-respect also. You just don't run away when you are in front of an obstacle. So if I believed it or not, I think it is irrelevant. I had to do it because there was still a chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But can you tell us whether you believed it or not, or did you not even ask yourself the question whether you believe it? You just acted because I think you thought that was the only thing to do, or was it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought it was my duty as representing the international community in Mostar at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. These were precisely the questions I tried to get an answer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, you said that the events that you described unfolded in Mostar between the 18th and the 20th. We just saw this one agreement, but let's look at another cease-fire, or let's look at another document which is 2D 00478, and that's the second document from the back of my binder. Please let me know when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is an order by the 1st Mostar Brigade. Just a moment ago you said that that previous order, in your view, was not professional enough. The date of the order is very important. That's the 20th of April, which is the same date when Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Petkovic signed that agreement in the presence of international observers and representatives of the international community. I would like to refer you to item 4 first, which reads: "Tasks which were given within the command for defence by the 41st Motorised Brigade commander, which relate to the anti-armoured company and PAM squad remain in effect." The items 1 and 2 refer to the implementation of the earlier order. In other words, they specify how the artillery should act upon the previous order. I'm sure you didn't know that such orders were being issued at the time you were in Mostar trying to form the commission and bring about a cease-fire in Mostar. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no knowledge of these orders, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to remind you of the order of the 19th of April that we referred to yesterday. Both these orders were signed by the same person, Commander of the 1st Mostar Brigade, Mr. Hujdur, and this brigade was definitely part of the 4th Corps. Now I wish to move on to some questions that will refer to the documents we saw. On the basis of these documents, and I also wish to remind you of the document we looked at yesterday --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very puzzled. If I remember correctly, the former order, we discussed the list of recipients, saying that it was also sent to the 4th Corps. Now you tell me that Midhad Hujdur is a brigade commander under the 4th Corps. So I'm very puzzled if he were giving orders to the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's impossible. To all military logic, it is impossible. He cannot issue orders to his corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday I showed you the order P 01970, and let me tell you this - I don't have much time - in the introductory part of which it was said that the 41st Motorised Brigade as well as elements of the units which were part of the 4th Corps were to execute the order. The order, or a copy of the order, was sent to large numbers of units for the execution of the order and for information, including the 4th Corps. I don't have much military knowledge, but I believe that where an order is issued by a unit within a corps, such an order has to be sent to the corps itself in order to be acted upon or for information. And I wish to say that without doubt this unit belonged to the 4th Corps. But let us not, either you or I, comment on these orders. I only wanted to point to you in a chronological order what was going on in Mostar, in the general area of Mostar, while talks were ongoing with a view to establishing a cease-fire. May I proceed with my questions now?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Based on the documents shown to you and the information you had, is it fair to say that there is no doubt that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period between the 16th and the 21st of April, 1993, planned and carried out attacks in the area of Central Bosnia? In saying this, I'm referring to the documents we saw yesterday, which had to do with Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer that, I would very much like to go through the orders once more to see if they are orders for readiness or executive orders. They obviously are not executive orders, because it should be carried out on a code. So there was a preparation for it, definitely, yes. But whether that meant that that was meant to go into execution or not is another thing. Military people do a lot of preparations and have plans for everything, and I look at the complexity of the order. It looks more like a plan and than an order. But it definitely looks like there was planning going on for action, and it was prepared also on a code word, having read it. So in that respect, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General, I didn't ask you about the orders related to Mostar. Rather, my question had to do with the orders connected with Central Bosnia. And I believe that on page 15, line 22, this is entered correctly in the transcript. I was going back to the report dated the 17th of April and the resulting orders. That's why I specified it had to do with that. Can we agree that military operations were planned and carried out in Central Bosnia in the period between the 16th and the 21st of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I also believe that there's no doubt about the fact which we just saw that on the 18th and 20th of April, 1993, two cease-fire agreements were signed, one in Zagreb and the other in Zenica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On the 19th and the 20th of April, 1993, in Mostar, Mr. Halilovic, chief of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the BH army, and Mr. Ganic, a member of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were both present there. They were both present in Mostar. This is also beyond any doubt, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you recall that Mr. Ganic and Mr. Halilovic, on the 19th of April, 1993, made a public statement for the media concerning the agreement reached on a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- as I said before, I don't remember if Mr. Ganic was present in Mostar, but I definitely think that Mr. -- General Halilovic made a statement for the media. Everybody made statements for the media that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This piece of information I found in your statement where you explicitly stated that had Mr. Ganic and Mr. Halilovic agreed with your proposal and that they were quite pleased and that subsequently they gave a statement to the media. This is in your statement.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. When I say they agreed, that must have been during the meeting with Morillon in Medjugorje when I presented my -- my ideas on how to go about it. This is where they agreed, and Halilovic was very much on the train to -- and positive to what I said. But I don't recollect that Ganic went down to Mostar, but he might have done that. I do not deny it, but I do not remember that he went down. It seems unlikely because of the threat, and he was rather scared about that, that we would -- that we would have brought him into Mostar that night, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I asked you whether the two of them together made a statement in Medjugorje. In your statement you did not say where this was, but was it in Medjugorje that both of them made a statement at the end of the meeting with Mr. Morillon? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. In those two days, and we're talking about the 19th and the 20th of April, 1993, two orders were issued whereby the 4th Corps planned attacks upon the area of Western Mostar. Do you believe that anyone in the 4th Corps had been able to do this without Mr. Ganic and Halilovic knowing about it? Both of them were in Mostar at the time these orders were issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to have counsel refer back to the two orders, and if we haven't seen them already to put them in front of the witness so the witness can see the two orders. Secondly, beyond that I think it calls for pure speculation by the witness as to what units in Mostar area might have done or been able to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Both orders were shown to the witness. The witness has just commented upon these two orders. These are orders under numbers P 01970 and 2D 00478. Both were shown to the witness. One is dated the 19th of April and the other the 20th of April. Now, as to whether the witness is only able to speculate about them or not, the witness can give his answer if he deems so. Of course, if the witness cannot provide an answer, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My question was -- I'm being warned by my colleagues to repeat it -- the question. There is no doubt about the fact that 4th Corps at the time when Messrs. Halilovic and Ganic were present in Mostar issued these orders. We know the functions discharged by the two gentlemen. Do you believe that the 4th Corps might have been able to issue such orders without Mr. Ganic and Halilovic knowing of them, especially in view of the agreements signed previously, and I'm referring to the cease-fire agreements of the 18th and the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I assume counsel agrees that same exact logic would apply to whether the HVO orders and plans could have been entered into without Prlic, Petkovic and Stojic knowing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that that was a classical question for redirect. The counsel should not be -- have started that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll be happy to ask it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. General, please try to answer the question put to you by Ms. Nozica, and it is the following question: Despite the fact that Mr. Halilovic and Petkovic had reached a cease-fire agreement behind everybody's back, the 4th Corps was in a position to make preparations for an attack without General Petkovic being aware of it. This is, of course, pure speculation, but you might have some idea about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I suppose you mean General Halilovic knowing about it and not Petkovic. There may be two options, I think. If you regard this as not an executive order but a plan, then I suppose that the brigade commander could make such a plan without the knowledge. But if it is an executive order, it's more unlikely that he should be able to do that. The second option is that these things were going on notwithstanding the fact that cease-fire documents were signed, with the full knowledge, and I think I cannot judge in this. I can say it is possible and I can say it is not possible. I'm not completely familiar how they acted and how the discipline and how the military efficiency in these circumstances were. In a normal army with standards, neither planning nor execution would take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I would like to interrupt you for a moment, and I would like also to ask a question from General Pellnas, and it is the following: That we have been dealing here with two orders. The first one here, it is the -- actually, number 1970, and I really believe that we have to clarify, through your help and assistance, that this order was meant really either for attack or for defence. Of course the very title of it, it says "Order For Defence," and in the preamble of that order, so to say, it is said that: "Due to the worsening of the general military and political situation in the territory of the Mostar municipality and because of the reliable information that the HVO units supported by HV are to attack the city of Mostar and its environs, I hereby order," and in the order at number -- paragraph number 1 says: "To take up positions for decisive defence with the task of defending allocated regions as follows." If we go further, then on page 4 of that order, in paragraph 7, it is the penultimate paragraph in the order, paragraph 7, and it says that: "In case the enemy approaches, stop him and open fire if the need arises from all weaponry on disposal simultaneously. Pay close attention to expenditure of ammunition and do not waste it." So I would like to ask you, General, looking at that order, in your view is it a -- how would you classify it? Is it an order for preparation? And previously you mentioned that of course military units usually make -- are making preparations for any eventuality. Or it is an order really for attack. So it is my question, because I believe it was the question also asked by Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think you ask too much of my military competence in a short time to -- in another language with a system I'm not familiar, but I will try to give some answers. Most of the points are definitely defensive tasks. "Take up position." It does not necessarily mean that you have to attack. It may be a position where you take up a position for a defensive matter. That supports the first line, "Order for Defence." There are, however, some -- yes, it is 1.9, when there is a task for capturing Elektro Herzegovina premises. Now, whether that is an order for attack or to take up a useful defence position, it could be both, actually. And then my -- my consternation is due to the list. It says "Just submitted to," so we don't know who received it as an order or just received it. And then if we go into 04 -- 00478, it was the one with the code words, where the Defence counsel stated that this long order we just have discussed should be put into action by a code word, which also makes me wonder of the real substance of this order and how it would be executed. So it is beyond my professional knowledge to really judge what worth this order has. It is mainly defensive thing, but there are elements in it which obviously need them to take something to be able to take up the positions. So I think that is the best answer I can give for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, just one last question because we need to move on. One question of a technical -- technical and military nature. If we have an offensive order from NATO, in the former JNA or in countries with a rather strong army, when an order is given to attack, should the hour of the beginning of the attack be mentioned in the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be, I think, some time lines given for such an execution, but if it was to start on a code word, then the code word itself could, and maybe it did, set the timing for the operation to start. But I'm not familiar with this way of giving orders. I think it's highly inaccurate and highly unprofessional, so I can't really answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I'm being told that you've used up two hours and 27 minutes so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only have one document to cover and one question. I tried to stay within the time allocated to me, but there were many interruptions. I have just another question which I believe is quite relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you said that you did not meet with Mr. Stojic earlier on. Let me refresh your memory. You may have forgotten this. Can you please look at document 4D 00471. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a report or a record dated the 16th of January, 1993, an abridged minute of a meeting held in the UNPROFOR headquarters. I apologise for the fact that your name wasn't spelt correctly. But is it possible that you may have forgotten this particular meeting when you indeed did meet with Mr. Stojic in January of 1993? I will refer you to some important information. The meeting took place on the 16th of January. We can see that you were present, as was Mr. Nelson, Mr. Ronksley, Bruno Stojic, and then Petkovic, Bozic, and Filipovic also on behalf of the HVO. Mr. Bozic greeted you, as did Mr. Stojic. He said that he was at your disposal for anything that might need to be done for you. You thanked him. You said that you had been there already for two months but that you spent most of your time in Macedonia. Has this refreshed your memory in any way? Do you now recall this meeting? Tell me that first and then I'll go through some of the matters that I believe are important. Has the witness not found the document? It's 4D 00 --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it. I have it. First, I should say that my answers saying I didn't meet Mr. Stojic any more was after the events in Mostar in April. That was the meaning of my --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's not what it says.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me be precise. I asked you whether you, before that, had ever had any contacts with Mr. Stojic. And when I say "before," I mean before the 18th of April, and your answer was no. Now, I allow for the possibility that you might have forgotten, but just tell us now whether you remember the following, and I'll remind you that you also wrote this in your book, that you were surprised -- well, I might have made a mistake. It should be 2D 471 for the document number. But anyway, as I was saying, just tell me whether you remembered this meeting or not. Were you at the meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I don't receive any more translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember this meeting, but I don't dispute it at all. I think this was probably when I had lunch with Mr. Prlic after in this -- at this timing, but I'm not sure. I don't remember this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we just briefly take a look at what happened at the meeting, because it's rather important for me to see whether you remember your impressions, the impressions you gave at the meeting. So if we take a look at page 1, you express your gratitude. You say you were in Macedonia. You say you would like to hear the assessment of those present of the talks in Geneva, and you say Mr. Stojic says: "I personally think cooperation was good on both sides and problems were sporadic. Mr. Bozic is in charge of the relations with UNPROFOR and the European Union, European Community, and I'd like to invite him to tell us about it while Mr. Petkovic is in charge of the military aspect." Then Bozic presents his views, says there's shooting going on. You ask, "What do you think? Who is shooting?" And then you go on to say, "Why is my team outside Mostar?" Mr. Bozic says, "That's your team's decision and they can be stationed in Mostar." And Mr. Stojic responds by saying, "We're at your disposal for everything that you require and then you go on to speak about the disproportion in teams on one and the other side and the increase in the number of teams on this side and you say that you consider your teams must be better supplied logistically, and they're passing from one line to the other. Mr. Bozic says that he's at your disposal for anything you might need to do, and then we have a lengthy address by brigadier Petkovic about the military situation, the situation in Geneva, and finally you say and you sound highly optimistic -- or, rather, you say about him you sound very optimistic. I would like others to do things the same way. And then at the end -- well, you can read the document. I'd like us to look at it together just to remind you and to confirm whether that was indeed the case and whether you remember the meeting proceeding in that way, and does this reflect your position and you expressed a very positive stance with respect to what the HVO was doing at that time and Mr. Stojic included, and finally it says you were invited to attend a luncheon which you accepted readily, and then it says in continuation Mr. Pellnas and his team met with Dr. Jadranko Prlic which would correspond to what you yourself said?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am now reading a document a vague recollection of this meeting, and I think the people in south -- the BH south, the UNMO, probably wanted me to have this meeting to make -- open doors for them in a better way. That must have been the aim of this meeting. And since it was the first meeting, obviously it had a social component; to be nice to each other. So I recollect, but it is vague. It is vague. The lunch with Mr. Prlic now falls into place. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So we can confirm that you did attend the meeting, and we can also confirm, can we not, that one tends to forget certain things. So one can't always be certain about making assertions because, of course, a lot of years have gone by since then. Thank you, sir. I think that I have been told that we have used up one hour and 30 minutes, which was the original time we were allocated, one hour for our Defence and 15 minutes from two other Defence teams. So I'm in the Trial Chamber's hands whether Mr. Murphy's going to be allocated more time, whether you're going to tell us now or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm little lost now as to what the remaining time is and whether I do have time. I'm very conscious of the position of the other accused, so I don't want to trespass on their time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I want -- I want to make very measured comments here and I don't want to make it directed to Mr. Murphy at all because these are not -- my comments are not personal to Mr. Murphy, who I have great respect for. The Chamber came in this morning and said the Defence total would have an hour and 40 minutes. I don't think that time can just continue to expand and expand and expand and if the Prosecution -- if I were bring in Mr. Mundis and Mr. Stringer and somebody else and said now I've used all my time, but now I want more time for Mr. Stringer or Mr. Mundis, I don't think that would be appropriate unless I allocated my total fixed time accordingly; but simply to be able to expand time, the allocated time, by saying now I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Stringer so he can have an extra 20 minutes; it's not appropriate. Now its up to counsel to allocate their time appropriately. I'm sure questioning from Mr. Murphy, it would have been helpful as it always is, but they could have allocated that time and planned that time among themselves. But instead we have a constantly expanding universe when it comes to the Defence time. The Prosecution works very hard to stay within the limits the Chamber imposes. The Chamber cut my time, the Chamber substantially cut my time, and I came in substantially less than what our original estimate was because I endeavoured to abide by the Chamber's direction. Now, I don't want to be put in this position. I don't like to be put in the position of complaining about these things. I don't want to appear stingy, but the Chamber puts me in the position where I have to rise to my feet and make the points that, with all due respect, the Chamber itself should police. So please let's have fairness to both sides. And if the Prosecution is going to be limited and the Prosecution is going to abide by the Chamber's time limits, then let's please have fair play, fair play. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, fine --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... to use up court time which is very valuable to us all, but I do think need to respond to the comment of Mr. Scott. I think that it is quite out of order to compare my colleagues Mr. Mundis, Mr. Stringer and Mr. Scott and other people from the Prosection with the six Defence teams present here, who -- which are completely independent and separate and do not wish, because that is not their functional, to allocate time or to cooperate in the way in which my learned friends within one team cooperate which is in fact the Prosecution. The Defence of General Petkovic, and I suppose that other Defence teams share my view, are not that interested in how much time other teams have at their disposal, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, sorry if I interrupt you, but you are basing what you say on a misunderstanding. I think Mr. Scott was only addressing the issue arising from one team speaking through the mouth of one counsel and then within the same team wishing to add time for another counsel. I think he did not refer to the different teams at all. Am I right, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that is the case, I apologise to my learned friend Mr. Scott, but I understood him to say differently and that's why I reacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In honesty, Your Honour, my points -- I made two points, one being within the team and one being more broadly but certainly I was about to say the same thing, Your Honour, in terms of -- the comments in terms of it's all within the same Prosecution team, well that again with all respect applies to the Stojic team, and they do both work for the same client. And again, I say nothing, I say nothing about how they should have allocated time among themselves, and I would invite Mr. Murphy, of course, his full participation as always. But it's up to them to allocate the time between themselves and not have more time added at the end thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me say a few words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please wait a moment, Ms. Nozica. Let me say a few words about time. The Prosecution has used up three hours and 30 minutes. We've decided to grant four hours and a half to the Defence because the Prosecution was granted 30 additional minutes. Within these four hours and a half for the Defence, the Defence has so far used three hours and 24 minutes. In other words, the Defence has one hour and five minutes left. The problem here is that we still need to hear Ms. Alaburic and Mr. Kovacic or Mr. Praljak, I'm not quite sure which one of the two, and we need to complete this hearing at a quarter to 2.00. My worry here is as follows: Of course, I'm always very interested in hearing comments and submissions by Mr. Murphy, but Ms. Alaburic, how much time do you need? How much time will your cross-examination last?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would be very satisfied if I were to have an hour and a half at my disposal. I would, of course, need more time to conduct my cross-examination, but in view of the circumstances, that would suffice. As far as I can see, we won't be able to be absolutely satisfied with the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak and I -- or, rather, the Defence of General Praljak had counted on the original 30 minutes, plus 10 minutes received from the Pusic Defence. That makes it 40 minutes, and we had hoped that of the additional half an hour which the Defence has been given, that we could be allocated at least 10 to 15 more minutes so that General Praljak could round off the set of questions that he had planned to ask. So if we were to be given a total of 50 or 55 minutes, we'd be very happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm totalling up your time, and if that is the case, then we would not have enough time, because after the break in 20 minutes we'll have two hours and 30 minutes left. The Prosecution has requested at least half an hour for the purposes of re-examination. In other words, the Defence only has two hours left. If Ms. Alaburic needs one hour and 30 minutes, Mr. Kovacic, 50 minutes, and if we add 20 minutes for Mr. Murphy, then it does not add up. Therefore, you need to find an agreement. So I think the best solution is for us to take a break. You need to consult each other, and of course you will have the time I said. Mr. Scott will start his re-examination at a quarter past 1.00 for a half hour of re-examination. So we're going to have a break now, and I will give -- then give you until a quarter past 1.00, and then Mr. Scott will take the floor. But please try to find an agreement between yourselves or amongst yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Let me greet Mr. Karnavas, who is back with us. And I'd like to ask the Defence counsel whether they've come to an agreement about the remaining time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Praljak will take 45 minutes. Counsel Alaburic will use five minutes less than the one and a half hours she was allotted, which means one hour and 25 minutes, which means that Mr. Murphy would have 10 to 15 minutes left, but otherwise we have no more time. And then the Prosecution could begin redirect, as you said, at 1.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Murphy, you will be granted 10 minutes, but no more than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My understanding is I will do that once the other accused have cross-examined. That way if this things go wrong, we don't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Who will start, Ms. Alaburic or Mr. Praljak's Defence? Yes, Mr. Praljak. Put questions of a military nature, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just military matters, and I'm sorry that we can't clarify them to the extent that we should like to. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at the document again, P 01970, the 19th of April order. And please try and give me brief answers because of the time constraints - yes, no, and so on. But let's start off by taking a look at the first sentence, "Pursuant to the order of the commander of the ABiH 4th Corps," et cetera. Does that sentence mean that the order as follows was made pursuant to an order of the commander of the ABiH 4th Corps? Is that crystal clear as the brightest summer day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at point 1.1, please, the second line. "Once conditions for that are met, launch an attack at the Mostar-Buna, Mostar-Blagaj junction," et cetera. Take up -- does that -- does it say "launch an attack" there? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, paragraph 1.2 next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Praljak, do not repeat this, asking the witness to affirm two words or three or a sentence which is in the document, because that is of absolutely no value. We all can read it, and you're losing your time. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, we've been discussing this at length, whether this order is a defence or an attack. If this document were clear, we wouldn't have any need to discuss it further. I simply don't know whether this document is clear or not, because in this document, according to military rules, rather -- regardless of whether they are written according to NATO standards or the standards of the Swedish army. It says according to this order what the BH army is intending to do on the 19th of April, 1993. And if that were clear here, then there would be no need for me to ask questions. But if it says here, as it does, that after the lines have been reached which have not within taken control of --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It sounds more like, if I here what's been said in the courtroom correctly, that Mr. Praljak says the document is not clear. The witness says the document's not clear. It seems to me the inquiry is at an end. Everyone agrees. The witness and the questioner agree that the document is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I might be allowed to say something. Mr. Praljak wanted to ask brief questions through the contents to lay the foundations in order to ask his question after that, once he had done that. So this is procedure, procedural tactics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I didn't say that the document was clear. I'm wondering why something that is crystal clear can be thought not to be clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General, in the background of the positions obtained to block the HVO forces and neutralise them. And then further on in the next line it says: "Carry out an attack from the flanks at Semovac, Podhum, Banovac, Centar 2 and Rudnik and part of the force is set aside to take control of Hum hill." Now, General, you have the map behind you where those positions are to be found. Do you know Mostar well enough in order to be able to testify that the map drawn there is very precise and shows the BH army's intention to take control of Rudnik, Hum, and the other locations on the map? Take a look at the map, please, and you will find the HVO positions clearly indicated there, too.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with Mostar enough to immediately look at the map and answer questions on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 1.8, the last line or penultimate line. It says: "Troops to be used in the attack on the MUP building and the Mostar police station are to be on standby in the Mostar Hotel." "... on standby in the Mostar Hotel," it says. Now, those forces, the troops referred to, are they the troops which, pursuant to a request from the HVO, you pulled out of Mostar which were supposed to take control of what it says here? Are those the same troops?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, that they are. They must be since the dates are very close. So these must be the troops that I took out. So obviously they were not to be used in the attack since they were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Because quite obviously by your presence you prevented the execution of this order. But look at paragraph 2 now, please, point 2, and the absurdity of the text as it stands. It says: "Be on standby for the defence by 1700 hours on the 19th of April, 1993, by which time the transfer of men and ordnance from one bank of the Neretva River onto the other should have been completed." Now, in military terminology, "standby for attack," does it mean that by such-and-such an hour all the units must be at the position for attack? Is that what "standby" means?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It actually says "standby for defence" and not for attack. And I don't know from which bank of the Neretva we are talking about. I don't understand it quite. If they are pulling back to the east of Mostar or if they are going over the river to the west of Mostar, it's not clear to me. I'm not trying to evade your question. It's just that I don't want to be pressurised to answer a complicated question in a minute with a document I'm not fully familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, General. Thank you. The transfer of manpower and ordnance from one bank to the other, from the right to the other, I don't think is in question, but I'll move on. Now, when you arrived in Mostar, did your assistants inform you about the military situation in and around Mostar facing the Republika Srpska forces, the deployment of sources? As a UN military observer, were you informed of the military situation in the city of Mostar and to the left and right of it? And looking at the map as well. That's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a very vague idea about the situation. It was not a good orientation given by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now may we have the next map on the easel.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just add one point I just noticed? Paragraph 7, last line: "Pay close attention to expenditure of ammunition." It doesn't seem to be an army just going to attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me what the logic there is, how you come to conclude that? Pay attention to expenditure is a classic form of order issued to any army not to waste ammunition, especially to an army that has ammunition shortages. So can you link this to defence or attack, the expenditure of ammunition? So could you explain that to me, please, and to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It takes a lot more ammunition to go to attack a position than to defend it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, undeniably, but tell me, what has the fact that somebody has to save ammunition if because of the embargo on the importation of weapons and ammunition there is a shortage of ammunition? You're making conclusions on the basis of logics which I fail to understand. If somebody is saving ammunition and paying attention to expenditure, that that necessarily means it is a defence operation rather than an attack one. I don't follow you there.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't make much conclusions. I just thought it worthwhile pointing at this line. It has some importance, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you for that observation. Take a look at the map behind you, the small map which shows the deployment of units. Green is the BH army, the red is the army of Republika Srpska, and the blue is the HVO. Did you know that the deployment of forces in Mostar at the point of your arrival was as it is indicated on the map, although other witnesses have confirmed that? Did you know the deployment of the forces of the three sides - the ABiH, the HVO, and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In broad line, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The south of Mostar was covered by the 3rd HVO Brigade. That's what it says on the map. Do you know -- did your assistants, who should have known the situation and the events, convey to you that in the 3rd Brigade of the HVO, 50 per cent of the composition was made up of Muslims in the HVO ranks? Did you know about that fact?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General, did you know that in the 2nd HVO Brigade holding positions north of Mostar facing the army of Republika Srpska, that 35 per cent of all the soldiers were Muslims, Bosniaks, wearing HVO uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you take a look at document 3D 00998.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you say again, please? 3D 00 --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The document is dated the 29th of December, 1992, and the commander of the operative zone, Brigadier Miljenko Lasic, is informing the Main Staff of the HVO what artillery weapons they have and number of tanks they have at their disposal. T-34, 7 tanks; T-55, 7 tanks, and so on. And the launchers, rocket launchers, 107-millimetre, 128-millimetre, and so on and so forth, they've been added at the bottom. Now, did the military observers ever send in reports telling you what artillery weapons and pieces the HVO had at their disposal in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And if they had knowledge of it, they would not have reported it in -- by means of communication. Hopefully not, because it could easily be snatched up and we would be accused of making intelligence. So these were the things that were probably not reported or taken in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General, you only need to tell me whether you knew of this or not.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please read this. One tank, T-34, is at the Konjic theatre in the ranks of the -- has been transferred there by the BH army units. Does it not transpire from this that in December of 1992, the HVO gave to the BH army one tank that was transferred to the Konjic theatre for the purposes of fighting the Serb forces there? Is this what this reads, and did you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm reading the right document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's the same document, 3D 00998. There is one remark beneath the list of artillery which says that one T-34 tank has been transferred by the -- has been transferred to the battlefield of Konjic by the BH army units. Were you aware of this and is this true?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware, and I don't know whether it is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You don't know that they were trying to lift the siege of Sarajevo there? Let's look at the next page of the same document, which is also dated the 29th of December, 1992. Well, you didn't know that that tank was used for the purposes of lifting the siege of Sarajevo. So the 29th of December, the next document, Colonel Zeljko Siljeg informed the Main Staff of the HVO of the artillery pieces he had at his disposal and they're listed under items 1 through 21. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it very hard to understand what documents from December has any bearing about the military situation when I enter Mostar on the 18th of April. Of course I have no information about the December situation when there was still war waged against the Serbs. So I cannot answer documents relating to December with the background of arriving there on the 18th of April. I find it useless to answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General, my question is a simple one. Did you know about these figures or not? We don't need your explanations. We've heard them. My question is simple. Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a look at the map behind you showing the disposition of forces. Can you testify that this is roughly what the situation was, as you were aware of it when you arrived in Mostar in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it corresponds to my rough idea about how the forces were located - the Serbs up in the mountains and the Croats holding on to the mountain ridge and the west part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can we have an IC number for the map and can we show the next map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have an IC number please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will become IC 596. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the map to be set up, I have this question for you: Do you know that after the BH army, based on your great efforts, left the Mostar Hotel, do you know whether the HVO personnel was transferred to North Camp in Mostar on the left bank of the Neretva? Therefore, is it true to your knowledge that the HVO, as per the agreement reached, went to North Camp and was to experience what we later saw they indeed experienced? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General, you're a professional soldier. On this map here, the one you see up there behind you, there is a modest plan of attack, as far modest as could be, which the HVO had to use to capture -- to have control of Mostar. You can see the different axes to the north, west, east, and south. Now, as a professional soldier, would you approve one such map of the HVO's possible attack on Mostar? And I'm asking you merely as a soldier, and this is a hypothesis, of course.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Part of the artillery that the HVO had in the different areas, if you were to attack Mostar, would you pull in some of the tanks into the town to destroy strongholds? Would you prepare logistics, communication systems? Would you bring in the back-up forces into the Mostar area? Would that form part of the normal procedure of preparation for an attack on Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an impossible question to answer in this time frame and with the things presented. I don't have the time; I don't know the map; I don't know the forces; I don't know the relations. I don't want to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is any of this, and you know nothing of this except for the fact that everyone knows who attacked Mostar on the 9th of May, 1992, based on the movements of logistics, artillery, and so on and so forth -- or, rather, was any of this information on any possible movements of units conveyed to you by your assistants? Did you talk about any such information there?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was quite a lot of rumours and information coming about movements in the Mostar area before the 9th of May, which I don't think much was substantiated or verified. But there were a lot of reports coming in about movements. I do not remember, actually. We --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you refer to a single report by the European observers or the UN military observers or UNPROFOR that would substantiate your words, except for the stories or rumours that you referred to? Any report, and can you cite the author of the report and the date of the report. Perhaps the Prosecution can be of assistance in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just a clarification of the question. Substantiate your words. Which words of the General did Mr. Praljak want him to substantiate? It's not clear to me and, I suspect, not clear to the witness. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Of rumours, if rumours went round. And we constantly keep hearing about rumours and stories going round, and I hope sincerely that we're speaking about facts here. Therefore, my question: Which facts, that's to say reports from UNPROFOR, European or UN military observers, do you have which would substantiate the stories of moments of HVO troops, tanks, artillery pieces, and so on and so forth would you be able to present here? I'm asking for at least one such fact.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is 14 years ago. I was under constant briefing in the UNPROFOR headquarters of all the regions in Bosnia, of all the events taking place in Croatia proper, and of course I cannot put forward one single report about this case, unless you present me with the actual documents or the situation reports from Mostar area. So the answer to your question is no, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the testimony of your military observer, he reached one particular position, at a bend, at 1200 hours on the 9th of May, 1993. Based on which fact or which logic could a general opinion have been formed that on the 9th of May the HVO launched an attack on the BH army in Mostar? I'm interested in the facts that led to that opinion and the logic which provided the general sense to these facts, all of which led to your conclusion, a widely shared conclusion, that on the 9th of May, 1993, the HVO attacked the BH army in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one of the facts that persuaded us that this was a planned action was the swiftness with which the people were taken first to the stadium and then brought to the helicopter factory. It was a very swift and efficient action. So it had all the bearings of a pre-planned action. I think this is one of the major things that made us conclude that it is well -- it was well-prepared. It was efficiently done.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General, look at this map of Mostar. There you will see a rectangle which stands for the Mostar Hotel and one rectangle which shows the position of the 4th Corps of the BH army and their 41st Brigade. That's in the depth of the western area. Can you locate these two features on the map?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can locate two rectangles, and I guess that the headquarters is the one closest to the river maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you mark that one closer to the river with number 1. That's the Mostar Hotel. And the other one which is closer to the bottom left-hand corner, which is the Vranica building. That's the staff of the 4th Corps and the 41st Brigade of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So do I understand, Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- Mr. Pellnas is to make the markings that Mr. Praljak tells him to make whether General Pellnas has any knowledge or evidence to give on this or not? He's simply to make the markings that Mr. Praljak tells him to make. I don't think that's appropriate. The witness has said he can't and doesn't know the map. He's not familiar. He can assume that some of the rectangles are certain things. The one closer to the river might possibly be the headquarters. I don't think it's appropriate to tell the witness what markings to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I would like you to indicate and mark number 1 and 2, those two rectangles which were military facilities. Did you know these locations personally, or can you not recognise these locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know of the locations for what they were, but I cannot locate them at the moment on this map. I will need a normal street map, I think, to be able to read other things. Even so, I think after 14 years if you had asked me to put money on betting which is Hotel Mostar and which is the headquarter, I would not probably put my money on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps it should be made clear for the record that what is referred to as a map is in fact not a map at all. It is an aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and in a rather bad shape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the witness cannot answer your question. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] That's sufficient for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: After having left the Mostar Hotel, the witness said in the examination-in-chief that he came with Mr. Pasalic to the Vranica building. In the Mostar Hotel there were some 60 to 100 people, and that's in the hotel and in the general surrounding according to what the witness said, which the HVO snipers had in their sights. My question is: How come the HVO snipers did not shoot and kill the staff of the 4th Corps, which is much closer to the HVO positions? Because until the month of September 1995, the people were able to walk through that area which was supposed to be the notorious area covered by the HVO snipers. Isn't it quite illogical, General, the fact that the Mostar Hotel was so blocked that the BH army was unable to leave it, whereas in the immediate vicinity of that area there were -- there was the BH army 4th Corps headquarters where people went normally about their business without being disturbed? Isn't that illogical?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is perhaps illogical, but I can assure you that General Pasalic was extremely scared running around Hotel Mostar. I didn't see any snipers. There was no sniping fire. But it was your commander of the operational zone telling me that they could not control your snipers outside Mostar. Having said that, I had to anticipate that there were snipers. They never denied that there were snipers around Hotel Mostar. On the contrary, they said they could not control them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General, that wasn't what my question was asking for, and I was asking you about the positions of the 4th Corps and about the fact that none of the staff there until the outbreak of hostilities in Mostar had been wounded or killed, but let's move on. In your statement, you said that as you went into Mostar the second time, you were using the road from the south and that you were appalled at the destruction inflicted on by the HVO forces. My question to you is the following: Did you ever use that road before when you were in Travnik? Did you go through Mostar to the east bank in daytime and see the devastation inflicted upon that area before the outbreak of hostilities there? In the month of April, did you cross that road and head along that road southwards?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite remember how we went. I came from Travnik and went down to Dubrovnik area. And how we actually passed the Mostar area I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If on the first occasion you used that road as you did the second time, how were you able to know which armies inflicted the damage or the devastation there; whether it was the HVO or the Serb forces? According to your statement, except for the pull-out of the BH army forces from the Mostar Hotel, except for that part, you did not go into east Mostar. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if we are discussing the sniper fire at my car, I base my assumptions on the fact that you don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General, please. Please.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The sniper fire --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the devastation you saw when you entered Mostar the second time. In a response to a question by the Prosecutor, you stated the devastation was quite extensive and you accepted that the HVO was responsible for that. If you were unable to compare the situation to what it had been before the outbreak of the conflict with the HVO, what led you to conclude that it was the HVO artillery that was responsible for the damage you witnessed there? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It was based and all the reports and all the situation reports we had at the time that the fire in East Mostar was mainly carried out by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Did a single assistant of yours stay in Mostar for the full 24 hours and, with military precision, count how many shells landed on the east bank and how many on the west bank and where the shells originated from? Did you, therefore, count how many shells landed and where they were fired from? And I'm just asking for a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no yes or no, because, you know, pretty well the UN observers were blocked from entering Mostar for a long, long time, during a number of months. It wasn't until the hostilities started to cease that we were able to enter, as far as I remember. I can't mention the dates when they were blocked and when they were let in again, but it was a long time, during the main part when the hostilities took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
