utterances.text: Very well. That's a different form of responsibility. But fact remains that if they were not there, they were unable to see where the shells were coming from and how many of them landed on the east and on the west bank. Is that right? They weren't there. They didn't know the facts. Is my reasoning logical, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. As you were heading toward the south on the second occasion you entered Mostar, you say you came under fire or, rather, an English officer told you that the fire was opened from the Hum hill; is that right? You said it was the -- the calibre was roughly 7.62.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He just pointed at the hill, and I don't know the name of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As a senior army officer, did you ask him how far the hill was removed from the road you were driving along? And that's the only road - I can't show it to you now - but that's the only road entering Mostar from the south. Did you ask him how was it possible for someone to fire with a weapon of 7.62 calibre from that position if that position was indeed that of the HVO? And did you ask him how distant that particular hill where the positions purportedly were was from the road? Did you ask him these questions?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know that between the road you were driving along and the foot of the Hum hill the BH army units were positioned? And that's to say they were positioned in the same direction from which the fire was opened. Were you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you not agree with me, then, General, that inferences were made on the basis of the broader picture, which was whoever opened fire upon UNPROFOR and European observers was the HVO? This is what the information was that came from Sarajevo and so on and so forth. There was no need to make any inquiries about it. Any fire that was opened from a range of a kilometre or a bit more came from the HVO. Nobody pursued this matter any further or made any inquiries about it.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have a point, but I don't think that I, in my book, have stated who actually sniped at us. I just made a statement that it was sniper fire. I hope that is the case. That does not contradict that I thought it was HVO, because my people said so, and they were the ones who knew the area and knew the sniping going on. So I had no reason not to trust this information. And we both know that the 4.62 millimetre will go about several thousand metres, but you won't be able to hit anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have two questions left. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can we have 3D 007958. This is the document dated the 10th of September, 1992, signed by Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you found it, General?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The document is relatively lengthy. I should like you to look at the first paragraph, somewhere in the middle, which says: "In the five months of war, the aggressor has not achieved its objectives, and because of the fierce fighting of the BH army and other forces, it was forced to stop at the lines reached." Now, the lines are mentioned as being those of Lasic, Kupres, Sujica, Podvelezje, Snijeznica, Hrgud. From what you know of the geography of the area where you were the military officer, do you know that Kupres, Sujica, Podvelezje, Hrgud, and so on and so forth, that all these localities were defended by the forces of the Croatian Defence Council and that it was solely the HVO that occupied those lines?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would object to this. I'm now asked to answer a question about a document issued even before I came to the former Yugoslavia. It was issued a month -- two months before I came down.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: General, that's quite clear to me on the basis of what you said. However, I'm asking you this: When you got there, your assistants and those who were your predecessors, did they prepare for you the maps of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the forces deployed on them? Did they inform you about the course of armed activities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, about the strength of the HVO and BH army units, as well as the strength of the Serb units? Did you receive any of that information as a soldier when you took up your position? Did you receive all the information that you required in order to properly discharge your duties in the area?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I most certainly went through a number of briefings all concerning the situation around the first week in November, which could have been completely different from the situation on the 10th of September. And I also -- because the briefings were not entirely concentrated to Bosnia. We had a lot of problems at the time in Croatia. I was sent immediately to Macedonia, which took up part of my time. So I would just say that you have a general knowledge, and there are so many facts, and this was a completely different situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. But anyway, we can conclude that you did not have an overview of what was happening from 1991 in Bosnia-Herzegovina onwards. Now, the document that I just showed you, which you say you are not able to comment on, in no part does Sefer Halilovic mention the HVO and what the HVO did in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you leaf through the document, and Their Honours will, too, there is no mention of the HVO anywhere. And my last question for you, sir, is this: Despite that, despite the fact that you did not have exact information about what was going on, here in the courtroom during the examination-in-chief you stated that the HVO units and BH army units together liberated Mostar, Stolac, Capljina, et cetera. Can you tell me now, how many soldiers did the BH army have participating in those operations and how many did the HVO have, roughly, or give us the ratio. How many was the -- soldiers did this joint force number expressed in figures?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I am very sorry that we can't bring in a military expert here to clarify some basic concepts here that we all need to know about and I think Their Honours, too, for us to be able to understand what this is all about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, General, good afternoon. I am Defence counsel together with Nicholas Stewart for General Petkovic, and I hope that over the next hour and a half I'll be asking questions that I consider to be relevant for our defence, and I'm going to start off with questions raised by His Honour Judge Trechsel, who, if I might be allowed to assess the value of the questions asked by a Judge, I consider to be very important and interesting. Now tell me General, the UN observers, did they consider the BH army to be an army which was defending Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were defending their own interests, which might in political level be Bosnia and -- united Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, please, when you say united, do you mean unitary? Or when you say united, did you have another concept in mind?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a concept. I think they had a concept for it, and that was their idea of it. And I don't think -- but then what my concept was is not interesting. It was what their concept was of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. But when you say that they fought for what you referred to as united Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'm interested in what you think they considered to be implied by the term "united."

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina ruled by some sort of administration in Sarajevo I think was in their interest. What that solution implied, and it depends on all the negotiations what -- that were going on. We had been shown numbers of examples from the Vance-Owen, the Stoltenberg-Owen negotiations. And I was asked yesterday if I shouldn't have known about the Vance-Owen Plan, and I should add to that it is natural that negotiators do not publish their documents because they have to keep it to their breast while they it are negotiating. So there were so many ideas about the united Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, did you consider the BH army to be a legal army on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you consider the HVO to be a and legal army on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell it us, please, do you have any knowledge to the effect that the conflicts in April 1993 between the HVO and the BH army were the first more serious conflicts between these two armies? If we make the exception of Gornji Vakuf for a moment in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except from the order, they started fighting in Central Bosnia. I think this was the first account between the two parts as far as I know it. Up till then, the Serbs had been the common enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But those conflicts in Central Bosnia that you're mentioning also took place in April 1993, did they not?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but a couple of days before maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So we can agree on that score, that before that there were serious conflicts in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993. Tell me now, do you have any knowledge about those conflicts?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little, because it was under the -- it was almost completely a problem for the Bosnia-Herzegovina UN command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that conflict ended with an agreement? And they agreed to cease-fire and an order was issued to cease the conflict.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, if within that context we now try to make a conclusion together, that is to say what somebody, including you, might have thought in April 1993 about the peace negotiations and attempts to effect a cease-fire through agreement, would it be logical to expect that both you and Generals Halilovic and Petkovic and other individuals considered this possible and realistic, that is to stop the conflict in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really answer that, because then I have to go into their souls and minds. If they wanted to stop it, I think they should have thought it could be possible to do it. If they didn't want to do it, then the question falls, and I don't know really what the real aims were from the two parties at this time. We were, anyway, very worried about -- that the conflict should start.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, you told us here that in April 1993 you did not believe in the possibility of a cease-fire to be reached through agreement and that in a way it was all a waste of time. I'm simplifying this in paraphrasing your words, but what I want to ask you is this: What would be the factual basis for the opinion in April 1993 to the effect that it wasn't possible to resolve the conflicts between the BH army and the HVO through negotiation and agreement?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was such a strong political division between Sarajevo and the leaders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. To my knowledge, not least Mate Boban and people in Zagreb who at that moment, I think, were on the verge of creating the independent state of Herceg-Bosna in one way or the other. And that was the basis, because I thought it would be difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, can I just ask the transcript be corrected that -- the witness has clarified he was talking about the independent state of Herceg-Bosna when he talked about the leaders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I take it that the reference was to the leaders of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, do you have any knowledge about the fact that Generals Halilovic or Petkovic would start negotiating a cease-fire without sincerely believing in that being possible and without investing their all to bring that about? So do you have any concrete facts?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us please, General, from today's standpoint, or maybe just a few years later after these events, can we jointly conclude about the intentions and possibilities that were open in mid-1993? Can we do that from that distance of time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we can do it better now than we could at the moment because we have the result of events. But that does not give us the right to judge what people thought two weeks before a certain event. So it is possible that there was an openness and that it could have happened, but the experience tells us otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move on to specific documents, and I see you have my set of documents before you. So I'm going to deal with the meeting of the 18th of April, 1993, in Mostar to start off with. In connection with this meeting, you said of General Petkovic that he refused to negotiate with Arif Pasalic because Pasalic was of a lower rank. Did I interpret your words correctly, General?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I understood that perhaps General Petkovic was not just referring to rank but rank with position. He was not in the position to negotiate about this. So it is a bad expression to say he was of too low a rank. He was not -- he had a rank, but combined with his position, it did not made it proper to negotiation with.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to interpret your words in the following manner, then: If General Petkovic considered that at that point in time the focal problem was Central Bosnia, while Arif Pasalic did not have authority and competence -- and competence over Central Bosnia, that it was precisely for that reason that he wasn't the proper collocutor to discuss military conflicts in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but I don't think he was even on the position to discuss it in Mostar with the military leader of Herceg-Bosna. So I give General Petkovic credit for his refusal in that way. I should have done the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us take a look at four documents now, General, that I have prepared for you to take a look at. I think we'll be able to get through them quickly. The first document is P 01205. We all have the documents, so we don't need to dwell on them for long. It is a letter from Arif Pasalic to his superior, Sefer Halilovic, and in the introductory portion Pasalic says that on the 19th of January, 1993, in the presence of the European Community, an agreement was reached with Mr. Petkovic on a cease-fire in Gornji Vakuf. From this document it would emerge that Mr. Pasalic and Petkovic had agreed a cease-fire in Gornji Vakuf. Can we agree about that, General?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first time I see it, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I think that most of the documents you're going to see are ones you're going to see for the first time, so I'd just like to draw your attention to that introductory part where Arif Pasalic says he made an agreement with General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we can trust Arif Pasalic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And if we can't trust Arif Pasalic, perhaps we can trust the European observers. So let us take a look at the next document, P 1215, in which in point 2 the following is stated, actually 2(A): "Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Pasalic agreed that in order to reduce tensions an order should be issued jointly by the BiH and HVO commands to the local commanders in Gornji Vakuf." So from this document, it would appear that Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Pasalic reached an agreement concerning Gornji Vakuf. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have two comments. Still we are --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I apologise, but can we leave the comments to the end for the time being, because I have limited time at my disposal and I'm not sure I'll be able to get through my cross-examination, and of course we'll welcome your comments later on. Let's look at the next document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm supposed to answer yes or no on things which I would just like to comment so there's some sort of background to my yes or no. I will be very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: General, the rules of this -- it isn't a game, of course, but it has rules like a game has rules, and one of them is that the witness may be required by the Defence on cross-examination just to answer yes or no, and possibly the Prosecution in redirect can solicit your explanations. Although it is very unpleasant for you, I quite understand this. I think Ms. Alaburic is entitled to have the yes or no answers without the commentary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that case, it's yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's take a look at the next document. P 1238 is the number. It's an order dated the 20th of January, 1993. And on the last page, if you take a look there, it was signed on behalf -- in the name of the HVO by Milivoj Petkovic, and in the name of the BH army, Arif Pasalic. So the document is P 1238. P 01238. It is an order, as I said, signed by Petkovic and Pasalic. I'm going to ask you my question after showing you the next document, which is P 01710. It is an order, once again, a combination of the Bosnian and Croatian language there, dated the 23rd of March, 1993, signed in the name of the HVO by Milivoj Petkovic, and for the 4th Corps of the BH army, Arif Pasalic. Now, General, unfortunately I don't have time to show you any more documents about the contacts, agreements, and cooperation between my client, General Petkovic, and Arif Pasalic. However, I do wish to ask you on the basis of these two documents whether it is well-founded to conclude that Milivoj Petkovic did indeed cooperate with Arif Pasalic on matters relating to the area of responsibility of the 4th Corps of which Arif Pasalic was in command.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Rank was obviously not an [Realtime transcript read in error "new"] obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How do you mean rank was an obstacle? [In English] It was not. [Interpretation] Yes. I was reading in the transcript, because in the transcript it says: "Rank was obviously new obstacle." Not an obstacle. Right. Thank you. Now, General Pellnas, my colleague Senka Nozica showed you a series of documents which indicated the conflicts that took place in Central Bosnia. From your answers here today, I conclude that now you do have knowledge that the conflicts in Central Bosnia were in fact something that was the burning problem of the day. Did I understand you correctly on that score?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. I'm not going to show you some of the documents that I've prepared in my binder relating to the activities of the BH army, but I would nonetheless like us to take a look at certain documents which I consider you might know about or you would have had to have known about. The first one is P 01942. It is a report by the European observers for the 18th of April, 1993. That is to say the day when the Mostar meeting took place. So let us take a look at the first section of point 1 where it says that fighting is taking place throughout the whole of the area of responsibility of BH Central Bosnia. The worst fighting and of greatest intensity is taking place within this area where both sides are using all available means against each other. And then it mentions Travnik, Zenica, Capljina, Mostar. And as far as Mostar is concerned, it says that the situation is dangerous and tense, but no mention is made of any combat action. Now, tell me, this document and the portion I read out. Does it coincide with what you know about Central Bosnia as the focal point of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at another document, P 9619 is the number, for us to see what my client might have thought on the 18th of April, 1993, what the focal problem was in relations with the BH army and the HVO. And in point 2 which relates to Central Bosnia of that comprehensive report by the Main Staff, it refers to attacks launched by the Muslim forces with the objective of destroying, routing the HVO in the area of the Lasva River valley. And because I don't have much time I won't go on with the documents -- or, rather, the sentences, but we can leaf through this document together and when we do so we shall see that in Central Bosnia at that period of time the HVO casualties were 31 soldiers and a large unknown number of civilians, and it is assessed -- I've been told that the number hasn't been recorded. 31 soldiers. Ah, you mean the number of the document, P 1961 is the document number. And the document I'm referring to is P 01961. The number of the document was mistakenly recorded in the transcript. And it is about the attack on the part of the Muslim forces in Central Bosnia. The portion relating to Vitez states as follows: That the most dramatic events occurred in Zenica. Tell me now, please, General, at the meeting of the 18th of April in Mostar a decision was made to go to Zenica in order to calm the conflict there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had already been decided before the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, this decision, was it made precisely because the most dramatic situation was taking place in Zenica as it says in this consolidated report?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but it is logic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Just one more document for us to look -- see the importance of Central Bosnia and one sentiment -- sentence from that document the number of the document is P 01981. Once again an ECMM document. And in the first sentence it says that the situation in Central Bosnia has deteriorated precipitously during the week. The conflicts between the Croats and Muslims have expanded considerably. Now, tell us, please, General, does this observation, and I think it does, coincide with what you told us about the conflicts in Central Bosnia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but it describes a completely different picture than General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, the different picture, but tell me this first: On the basis of these reports and your subsequent information about Central Bosnia being the focus of the conflicts, would it be logical to conclude that the Croatian delegation at the meeting held on the 18th of April did not insist upon resolving the problem in Central Bosnia in order to draw attention away -- draw attention away from Mostar as you said but, rather, because Central Bosnia was truly a crucial problem?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say they tried to. I say I experienced it from my point of view looking upon Mostar as the most important part, as an effort to draw attention away from Mostar. I experienced this like that in my negotiating situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I'm not quite clear now on what you're saying. You said you didn't say that the Croats tried to draw attention away from Mostar but that that's how you experienced it, that you thought they were drawing attention away from Mostar. So your experiences and your opinions as presented here, your positions and stands, need not correspond to what actually happened. Would I be right in understanding you to say that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It was -- you base your thinking about what you're out to -- to achieve. I was there to achieve to get Mostar into negotiating, and they kept talking about other things. And they may have had all the reasons in the world for doing that, but in my situation I was not able to accept those facts fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. I understand. You didn't have sufficient information, so at that point in time you didn't realise the importance of Central Bosnia. Now, I don't wish to burden you with documents from the BH army because my colleague --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not what the witness said. The witness didn't say that that he didn't have sufficient information to say. He gave an answer, and it shouldn't be recharacterised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Alaburic, I was thinking exactly the same thing. The witness has not said in his conclusion what you've just said yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree that my sentence was inappropriate, but I believe that the witness said this because he confirmed here that it was only subsequently that he learned of the problems in Central Bosnia. Nevertheless, I apologise to my learned friend, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Still, we can clarify this, General. Did you at that time in April of 1993 have relevant knowledge of the events in the area of responsibility of both the HVO and BH army and that Mostar was not indeed the focus of the problem?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information to this sort, yes, but I stayed to solve the Mostar problem. So that was my focal point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I fully understand that. Let us look at two documents of the BH army which I believe can help us clarify matters further. The first one is 4D 599, which is a combat report by Esad Ramic from the 4th Corps. I wish to draw your attention to the very end of the report, to the very end of the penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have the number once again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. 4D 599.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat report?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's the last document, yes. Look at the very end of the report, the penultimate paragraph, which says: "There is no doubt that this is the case of an open aggression of Serbs and Croats against a sovereign Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We will finalise its liberation toward the east and west. Please do not stop us, and do not send us any negotiators." The report goes on, but I will not read that since it is not relevant to my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, can we agree that if what this combat report says is true, and it's dated the 17th of April, 1993, that the BH army was resolute in its decision to carry out attacks in order to, as they put it, liberate Bosnia-Herzegovina from Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us look at another document, 4D 00089, again by the commander of the 41st Motorised Brigade of the BH army, Mr. Hujdur. This order which falls into context with the order that my learned friend Nozica showed you, shows that, so it seems, on the 20th of April Mr. Hujdur issued several orders relating to preparations for certain combat actions. At that point in time, General, you were helping pull out the BH army from the Mostar Hotel. At that time you believed that the BH army was honouring the agreements that had been reached with them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had every reason to believe that, even if there was obviously strong divisions among them about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Finally, in relation to this meeting, I would like to put the following question to you: If we agree that Central Bosnia was the crucial problem and that Arif Pasalic was not the competent commander for Central Bosnia, isn't it logical for the Croatian delegation to be insisting at that meeting, in particular my client, General Petkovic, that the negotiations continue with Sefer Halilovic, man number one of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now that we've come to the issue of Mostar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As we are with this document, maybe you will again say that you cannot answer the question, but you were asked the same question with regard to other orders. Does this order look to you like an order for attack or preparation of attack or any other operation that could be characterised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm a bit confused because in paragraph 4 it says that they should be carrying out the combat operation on the code word RAK-625, which obviously refers to the long, long order which was issued on the 19th, I believe it was. So it's a number of orders, and I can't really judge how serious they are and in what context they are doing. This "You will infiltrate behind the enemy lines," that could be part of a defensive operation to disturb the enemy. But "Carry out attack in the direction of Hotel Mostar" is definitely then an offensive action. So this order contains both sides, and I don't like to comment upon it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic. Cross-examination by the Accused Petkovic:

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one question. It seems to me that when documents are being read, that those items that speak about facts more than the witness wishes to speak are diverted from. Item number 1 says that an attack has been launched and that the headquarters of the 41st Brigade have to be reached. The witness knows the distance between the Bulevar and the 41st Brigade's headquarters. This is several hundred metres that have to be covered in order to cross the distance. Isn't that right, sir? How else would you have come to the headquarters of the 41st Brigade other than by forcing the HVO forces from -- to pull out of that area? And I'm speaking of the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they really intended to go forward to the headquarters, then it would be attack, definitely. If you didn't -- if you were not in the mind of letting them go there peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Evidently you always wish to add something more. The second question: Infiltration between the enemy front line constitutes defence to you. Is that according to the NATO standards? You are pulling out forces into the east bank, and they wish to transfer their forces to the west bank. Since when does a sabotage line deep behind the enemy lines constitute defence according to NATO standards?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know so much about NATO standards, but I can assure you that in Swedish defence of our nation we would definitely take up action behind enemy lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another question. Don't you realise that while you in Mostar sent Lasic and Pasalic to sign an agreement, did -- did you do that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I received an agreement by them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the same time while Pasalic was signing an agreement with Lasic and troops were going into the barracks, his brigade commander, with his approval, was planning something quite different. Isn't that obvious from the documents?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, another question. Did you, perhaps, and other representatives of the international community who came to Mostar, General Morillon, Mr. Thebault, and Mr. Halilovic, did you prevent these orders from being materialised in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With what should I have prevented that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: With your presence and your talks.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can I say? I did my very best. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you haven't exactly answered the question put to you by General Petkovic, a very relevant question. The question runs as follows and I'll put it to you again: You were there, conducting negotiations with the parties to achieve a cease-fire and taking actions for that purpose, and here we have document after document that seem to be establishing that the ABiH in the back of the negotiators, so to speak, are preparing an offensive action. And the case of the Defence is that this operation was to be launched, was to take place, and General Petkovic is now asking you whether the fact that General Morillon, Mr. Thebault, and yourself were there on the spot in Mostar on that 19th day of -- 19th of April, 1993, did that not prevent the ABiH from conducting its attack? What can you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, we had, of course, no knowledge of any such planning taking place. I found on my account that Pasalic was more cooperative than HVO, which could have been wrong. Secondly, I personally forced the Spanish Battalion into Mostar against their will. And there was later a question in the Security Council if we had acted against the mandate, because the Spanish Battalion had only a mandate to support the logistic transports from the coast up to Sarajevo. That was their task. And they were not willing at all to interpose between the parties. So considering, I think, I did more than anyone could expect. And Morillon and Thebault immediately left for Zenica. There were no military resources. And I reported afterwards to my commander that unless we took action there would be a war in Mostar, and there were no actions taken to stop this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a small point of clarification. You said, "I personally forced," it's on line 15, "I personally forced the Spanish Battalion into Mostar against their will." Whose will are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The Spanish Battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, you're telling us that Mr. Pasalic was cooperating more than Lasic and others from the HVO, that he was more forthcoming. I wish to present to you a part of the testimony of one of the witnesses we heard in this courtroom on the 18th of January, earlier this year. This was protected Witness CV, who was at the Mostar Hotel as one of the soldiers you were pulling out of there. At page 12593 of the transcript, he told us that admittedly they pulled out of the Mostar Hotel, but that next they changed into civilian clothes and returned to the area of Cernica, to the separation line there. He said that they had changed into civilian clothes because as soldiers they were not allowed to move about pursuant to the agreement, also thanks to the mediators. Did you know that these soldiers whom you helped move out of the Mostar Hotel changed into civilian clothes and went back to the separation line?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like us to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, it's 10 past 12.00. We need to have a break now, a 20-minute break. We will resume at half past 12.00. According to my calculations, you will then have until five past 1.00 or 10 past 1.00 to conclude. I'm not sure whether Mr. Murphy will be able to take the floor, because Mr. Scott needs 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we start, if I may take one moment just in case we run out of time. It's on a slightly different matter. The Prosecution filed a -- a motion under -- oh, for the UN -- for certain UN documents to come in, additional documents, 47 documents to come in. It was filed, I believe, on the 29th of May, if I'm not mistaken. We would like to file a joint response. There will be several annexes to that with each Defence team individually responding to the 47 documents, but there would be one sort of joint response to the legal arguments. Could we have until the end of the month? We could have until the end of the month as an extension, because the documents are rather lengthy, and in order for us to go through them, and the Prosecution has provided rather specific answers as to why the documents should come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have considered the matter, and we grant your application. You will have until the end of the month to respond, unless Mr. Scott wants to object. Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, under the time -- unfortunately, under the timing that we're all working under that seems to me to be an extremely long period. That's a better part of the month. If that's what the Chamber wants to do, but I-- that does concern me. There's going to be a number of Prosecution filings like that in the next few weeks, tendering documents, and of course those will all have to be dealt with before the Prosecution can rest its case, and if we give a month here and a month there, then that takes a lot of time. Obviously, again as I said with Mr. Stewart yesterday if, you know, again if we can expect such extensive Defence responses, then I anticipate the Prosecution will seek leave to reply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then you will file replies when time comes to do so. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, on Monday you said about my client, this is recorded on page 61 of the transcript of the day, that on the 30th of April a meeting was held in Zagreb where you explained the proposal jointly put forth by the Joint Command of the BH army and the HVO. You said that General Petkovic was not actively participating in the talks, and you concluded on the basis of that that he was not interested in the subject of the meeting. Have I interpreted your words correctly?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at document P 02155. This is a joint order by Generals Petkovic and Halilovic, issued on the 30th of April, 1993, in Zenica. Tell me, General, does it appear from this document that on that date Generals Petkovic and Halilovic were in Zenica? I see that the witness is still looking for the document. The document number is P 02155.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. You see that the document is quite simple. It's an order. Generals Petkovic and Halilovic jointly issued the order. It says Zenica, the 30th of April, 1993. Have you found it, General?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at it together. Does it emerge without any doubt from this document that on the 30th of April General Petkovic was in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it not logical that if he was in Zenica on that date he could not have possibly been in Zagreb at the same time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, then, that your statement referring to that meeting taking place in Zagreb on the 30th of April, 1993, cannot stand because on that date my client, General Petkovic, did not attend any meeting in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date I stated was obviously wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Before we try to establish what the actual date was, let us look at the order that I referred you to. Can we agree that the intention behind this order is to materialise the agreement within the framework of a Joint Command of the BH army and the HVO? We can see that this relates to the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps and the operation zone Central Bosnia. The seat was supposed to be in Travnik. Let us not read it any further. Can we not agree, therefore, that this order refers to the implementation of the agreement on the establishment of a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us try and find out what was the meeting you were referring to. My colleague Karnavas asked you yesterday whether you were mistaken in believing that it was the 30th of April. He suggested that it may have been the meeting of the 24th of April in President Tudjman's office in Zagreb. Your answer to him was, "Probably, yes."

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not in President Tudjman's office. We were at Intercontinental Hotel in Zagreb with this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you're talking about the meeting of the 24th of April?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously I'm not certain of the date. I'm just referring to the meeting during these days that took place under the leadership of David Owen and Vance and when Brigadier John Wilson and myself met Petkovic and Halilovic discussing the matters of a joint command in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let us look at document P 02059. P 02059. These are minutes from the meeting which took place in President Tudjman's office. This meeting -- at this meeting a previous meeting between Generals Petkovic and Halilovic was referred to. I would like to draw your attention to these relevant portions of the minutes to see whether this was indeed the meeting we were interested in. Let us look at page 4, paragraph 5. I will be interpreting from the English text, and I apologise if my interpretation is wrong. "Generals Petkovic and Halilovic have spent several hours together this evening along with three objective, impartial advisors, more precisely two UNPROFOR generals and my personal military advisor" - that's what Lord Owen says - "and my personal military advisor." Therefore, they spent several hours together. What follows next is John Wilson's intervention or speech, and I will be quoting it in English: "[In English] There was an exchange of views between General Halilovic and General Petkovic with some remarks on our part." [Interpretation] It goes on to paraphrase the substance of the agreement, and at the end of page 5: "[In English] The conclusion of both General Halilovic and General Petkovic was that they would need certain political guidelines with regard to command and coordination. That is also another issue which refers to the political level from which such instructions would come. And my final remark, Mr. President: I think that if they get the right instructions, they will be able to solve all technical and military problems and issues clearly and appropriately." [Interpretation] Before I put my question to you, I will show you one more detail from the minutes. On page 35, the words uttered by Lord Owen were recorded, paragraph 3 from the bottom of the page, which says: "[In English] For several months I talked both to General Petkovic and General Halilovic. I monitored their participation in talks. I received reports from their joint meetings, and I had the feeling that they could lead and command in the operational sense together." [Interpretation] Tell us, please, General, these conclusions presented in this transcript, do they correspond to what went on at the meeting between Generals Halilovic, Petkovic, and the military representatives of the international community in Zagreb on the 24th of April -- or, rather, the 20th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Because I don't have much time, I'll conclude with the details. I find that answer satisfactory. Now, General, let us take a look at what it was that Generals Petkovic and Halilovic did in that third decade of April 1993, believing that they could bring about peace in the area. My colleague Ms. Senka Nozica showed you their agreement dated the 20th of April in Zenica. I would now like to take a look at what happened in the ensuing days, so to do that, let's take a look at document P 2016. It is a document of the European Monitors in which on page 2, towards the end, mention is made of Central Bosnia, and it is said that Busovaca and Gornji Vakuf joint commissions [In English] "... continues to be challenged and are doing excellent work." [Interpretation] I'm going to skip over the next portions and look at the 18th of April, on page 3, last passage where it says: "[In English] The result was the establishment of two joint operation commissions consisting of ECMM, UNMO, HVO, and BHD in Mostar and Zenica. The first meeting was held on the 19th of April in Mostar after several preparatory meetings." [Interpretation] And now on page 4. I don't want to read it because it's a lengthy passage, but we can see what they are trying to do in Zenica, that is to say, Generals Halilovic and Petkovic, what they're trying to do. So the second and third portion on page 4. And in conclusion, following the agreement: "[In English] In the morning of 20 April, General Morillon, Vice-President Ganic, ECMM, UNPROFOR, together with HVO and BH military and civilian representatives, went to Zenica to establish the Zenica Joint Operation Committee." [Interpretation] Tell me, please, General, from this document, does it indubitably emerge that Generals Petkovic and Halilovic, along with the assistance of representatives of the international community, did in fact go to Zenica in order to implement the agreement on the establishment of a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now take a look at a joint statement by Izetbegovic and Boban on the 25th of April, and it is document P 02088. It is a document compiled on the basis of a conversation, the transcript of which we were looking at a moment ago. We've already seen this joint statement in this courtroom a number of times, so let us focus on attachment 1, the military attachment, signed by Izetbegovic and Halilovic on the one side and on the other Boban and Petkovic. So, General, let us look at point 1 which states that the BH army and the HVO will retain their individual identities and the establishment of their commands, and in point 2, they will set up a Joint Command which will be responsible for controlling operations of the military districts. On number 3, the Joint Command will consist of two Supreme Commanders, Halilovic and Petkovic, et cetera, et cetera. Now, tell me, General, did you know that on the 24th -- between the night of the 24th and 25th this document was signed and that in fact the parties decided at top level to form a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And did you know about the joint statement that was signed on the basis of this agreement in the presidential offices of President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Am I understand you correctly? Are you saying that you knew about the joint statement but not the military attachment to that joint statement? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, but I'm not quite certain about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let us take a look at what my client did on the following day together with Mr. Stojic. So look at document P 2097. And you will see in the introductory part that the signatories are representatives of the defence department Bruno Stojic and General Petkovic, and they are referring to the agreement that we looked at a moment ago reached in Zagreb on the same day, and they are issuing an order by which all offensive action is to cease, that there should be a cease-fire. And let me ask you, General. Do you know that the Croatian side issued the necessary orders straight away with a view to implementing the agreement reached in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let us look at the next document, which is P 02114. It is an appointment by General Petkovic, dated the 26th of April, 1993. Once again in order to implement the agreement reached in Zagreb, and it relates to the appointment of individuals to the Joint Command of the HVO and the BH army. At a general level, then for Mostar, Central Bosnia, and Tuzla. Tell us, General, did you know that the Croatian side immediately undertook the appointment of its representatives to the Joint Command in conformity with the agreement reached in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document. 4D 00333 is the number. And it is a joint order by Generals Petkovic and Halilovic, dated the 29th of April, 1993, also in Zenica, on the release of all detained civilians and the sanitization of the battleground. Tell me, General, did you know that Generals Petkovic and Halilovic, towards the end of April, were still in Zenica in order to try and put the agreement on a peaceful solution to the conflict into practice?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, if we cast a glance back on the basis of this -- these documents, would it be proper to conclude that from the 19th of April to the end of April General Petkovic was with his colleague General Halilovic throughout that time and that in Zenica and Zagreb they endeavoured to find a peaceful solution to the conflict between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would conclude that orders were given to this, or at least formulated to this extent it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I now have two more topics which I think I'll have time to go through. General, you told us that it was agreed that four teams be set up to tour the crisis spots in Jablanica and Konjic, the Jablanica and Konjic areas, and one of these teams set out towards Doljani, came across a group of soldiers wearing black uniforms who had swastikas on them. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, where do you get this information about the swastikas from?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Major Grant Finlayson, my New Zealand UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That man was heard here as a witness, General, and he made no mention of any swastikas, nor did we in any other document come across this piece of information according to which certain soldiers wearing black uniforms also supported swastikas, so can I ask you whether you -- whether you can with certainty that you received information about these swastikas, or did you conclude that in view of the fact that these people were wearing black uniforms? Did that lead you to conclude that they also had swastikas?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that did not lead me to that. I must have had the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Finlayson and others, were they together with the representatives of the Spanish Battalion? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did they happen to set out towards Doljani then?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We formed teams, and they were accompanied by officers, as far as I know, from the BiH and the HVO. I'm not aware of any officers from the Spanish Battalion. If that was the case, it was without my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you some documents, and since they are documents which are protected, which are under seal, I'd like us to move into private session. The first document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for thinking about the public, it would appear, more than the present Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But anyway, it would appear, Witness, that you positioned armoured transporters in the night between the 21st of April. The Muslims managed to keep themselves there up at the line on the west bank. Do you agree with that, General? Do you remember it and would you confirm it today as well?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We positioned along the line agreed by the parties, and I of course then anticipated that this was the division line between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now to wind up, General, let us look at document 4D 00557, in which Arif Pasalic, on the 20th of April, 1993, informs his superiors and in so doing mentions what we discussed a moment ago, that the line, he says that in point 1 --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, is this 557?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [In English] 557, yes.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is reporting that on the 20th of April, a meeting of the representatives of the BH army and HVO was held, and that in the first point it was agreed to set up a separation line along the axis of Semovac, Bulevar, and Mose Pijade Street. Tell me, to the best of your recollections regardless of the passage of time, is that indeed the separation line that was established at the time and which was held until the end of the conflict in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank Your Honours for giving me extra time. I just have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It is this, General: General, have you heard about an offensive entitled Neretva 93; and, if so, what were the objectives that were supposed to be obtained with that BH army offensive?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can only say that Neretva is a very strategic valley opening up for the Adriatic, and of course that was of big value both for the Croats and could be for the BiH if they wanted to have access to the Adriatic. So Mostar is a strategic defence point for such an action.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you're saying that you don't know about this offensive, an offensive under that name.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, and I'd especially like to thank you for extending my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you would like to take the floor, Mr. Murphy. You have until a quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You're a very experienced military officer, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm an old officer anyway, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You were commissioned into the Swedish army, I think you told us, in 1961.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did Grant Finlayson serve under you as a United Nations military observer?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did you form any opinion about Mr. Finlayson's professional capabilities in that position?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: What was that opinion?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he is extremely stable, psychologically, mentally, and I trusted him 100 per cent. He was one of my best in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Is it important at all in your opinion for a United Nations military officer to be impartial as between the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a principle, yes, but it is also important to stand up against war crimes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But you would agree that it's important for a military observer to demonstrate an impartiality as to the issues in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And not to give the impression of taking sides?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not -- not while you are serving. You definitely should not try to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: May we go into private session just for a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I just have one or two questions, General, further questions about your operation in evacuating the members of the armija from the Mostar Hotel. You gave evidence that for the purpose of transporting some of the soldiers you made use of an ambulance or at any rate an APC marked with Red Cross insignia.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: On the face of it, that would not be a proper thing to do, would it?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot use the Red Cross transporting in a wartime, but my legal viewpoint in a split-second decision was that we were not in war and I was making this with the consent of both parties. So that was my legal defence for it. Perhaps shaky, but that was what I took at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, it was that answer about not being at war that I wanted to come back to. You also testified that you arranged for General Pasalic to wear a blue United Nations helmet during that operation.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That's also something that on the face of it is not a proper thing to do. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree. It's not the proper thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: The explanation you gave for that was that you wanted to keep him alive.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and above all I wanted to keep his head above the protection so he could guide us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you see any contradiction there between that answer and the answer that it was okay to use the ambulance because you were not at war?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends -- it hangs on the definition of "war." If snipers are shooting, if that is war, then perhaps. But on the other hand, we were not a party of the war, if it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. I need to move on very quickly. In 2003, General, did you give an interview to a Swedish newspaper called Aftonbladet?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Perhaps?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Let me remind you. Did you at any time make a comment to a newspaper in Sweden to the effect that the United States, and I'm going to use the words attributed to you, "had fabricated evidence against Slobodan Milosevic"?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You did not?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Madeleine Albright showed photographs in the Security Council concerning my border mission, which we knew at the time could not have been taken at this time and the spot they were produced to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. For reasons of time, I'm going to just quote from a document that is available on the internet, and I can put details on the record later. The interpreters do have it, so I'm going to, on the first page of this document, the fifth paragraph down, I'm going to quote what is said in this report from Aftonbladet. "In an interview with Sweden's leading newswire, TT, retired Brigadier Bo Pellnas claims that the United States faked evidence to suit their own interests." Did you use those words, sir?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- the base for this is an article I wrote for Dagens Nyheter, and if we are to quote me, one has to take the article in Dagens Nyheter and not quoting one of our worst papers in Sweden. But I stand by the fact that Madeleine Albright presented in the Security Council photographs which we fully believed were not taken on the spot or on the date which they were presented with. And I went immediately to the American ambassador in Belgrade and to the British ambassador and asked to have the photographs so we could act on it, and we were never given any further comments on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, the only the -- the only purpose of my asking this question is this: I'm sure you're aware that until his death last year Mr. Milosevic was an accused in front of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic was not involved in this process at all. It was completely between Madeleine Albright or the United States and my border mission, which was a border mission set up by the International Conference in the Former Yugoslavia. It has absolutely nothing to do with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. One final matter then. In your experience as a military officer since 1961, have there been occasions other than the former Yugoslavia where you were in a situation where people were shooting at each other?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: At any time during your service since 1961 when in those kinds of situations, have you ever heard people -- have you ever had a person threaten to kill somebody else other than on the 18th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Never?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not by words, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Not in all that time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Whatever Mr. Stojic said, by the way --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they have killed each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Whatever Mr. Stojic said, by the way, you heard through an interpreter, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour, very much. I have no further questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, Mr. Murphy mentioned to you the issue of the photographs. We know nothing about this whatsoever. What were these photographs --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- all about?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It has to do with a completely different thing. It has to do with my border mission when we were to check whether the Yugoslav government had closed the border to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there was a lot of criticism about this, because if they -- we confirmed that they had done, then sanctions against Serbia and Montenegro would be lifted. So there was quite a lot of interest to make sure that they were not fulfilling their obligations. And the photographs were at the check-point where we had observers 24 hours a day, and probably -- most probably also American observers. And so we concluded that the photographs were taken on another occasion. I used this when I wrote about the opening of the war in Iraq as an example that also democratic States sometimes use evidence in the Security Council which are not fully correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this had to do with the US looking for a pretext to actually engage NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, what is the relevance of all this? My time -- I hate to think that this is just simply to provoke further questions - and including questions from the Chamber - using this time photos on an irrelevant issue about photos about -- at the border on some other period of time which have nothing to do with even the credibility of this witness. That cannot even be the basis. So I object to this entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Earlier I just made a request for an extension of time to respond to 47 documents, UN documents, which the Prosecution wants to bring in as if they are true, accurate, and correct. Now we have a witness for the very first time who on several occasions has indicated that misinformation or wrong information often is presented before the Security Council. I think it is vital, and I wish to thank the gentleman for coming here and providing that very vital information to us. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, General. In your own chain of command, who were you accountable to? I thought I understood that you were under the authority of Mr. Wahlgren, who was in Zagreb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Now, as for the mission of the UN observers on the ground, we saw a document that was produced when Mr. Grant Finlayson, your colleague, came to testify. It was Exhibit P 487. We might show this document on screen, on the screen. It's document P 487. You don't have it in your documents. It was used with another witness, and in that document there was the definition of the mandate of the observers. They were to patrol to ensure a liaison between the parties, conduct negotiations, and support humanitarian missions. But there's something that I found extremely telling in this document. At paragraph 6 it was stated that the observer teams were placed under the operational control of each battalion. I believe that -- or when listening to you, I heard you make a few comments about the SpaBat. Were the observers independent from the battalions, or were they under the control of the battalions? Because that's what seems to be meant in this particular document that was produced on the 16th of September, 1992, by General Wilson.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were under the control of the battalions who could issue orders and task them. The only thing they would do was the reporting, but I was also responsible for manning of the -- of the observers and the personnel matters. And I certainly had a great influence on how they were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the battalions were in a position to give you orders. What type of orders are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could direct the UNMOs where to patrol, for example, and where to take up positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. There are many other questions I could put to you, but I don't want to take any of Mr. Scott's time. Mr. Scott you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, we're going to have to move fairly quickly here and hopefully I'll just be able to put a few questions to you. In connection with your knowledge of the -- what was happening in Mostar during -- around this time, and when I say "around this time," at the moment I'm talking about the spring and the summer and indeed into the fall of 1993. Mr. Karnavas asked you a question and the word he used was that essentially everything you knew about Mostar at that time was based upon your "excursion" in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mischaracterisation of what I said. He can quote from the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right at page 33, line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, in order to avoid any problem, you know that as soon as you start re-examining witnesses the Defence counsels get on their feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please quote the exact words of the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not sure I can do that in every instance but I will try. I don't think that's absolutely -- I don't think that's necessary, but I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On page 33 of yesterday's transcript, starting at line 22, Mr. Karnavas's asked this question to Mr. -- to General Pellnas: "So what I'm saying when you refer to your excursion the universe, if we want to put it that way, of your experience, hands on experience, in dealing with Croat-Muslim problems was that period when you went in April 1993; correct? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could we get the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the answer was "Yes, correct."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my coming back to you, sir, I don't think -- perhaps you sell yourself a bit short. Sir, you've shown us on a number of instances, is it correct that both before and after your time in Mostar on that occasion that you were receiving virtually daily reports from both UNMOs and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but we also learned today, somebody refreshed my memory that I was obviously down there having a meeting with General Petkovic and Bruno Stojic before this event on the -- in April. But because we had daily reports, but I must admit they were not focused necessarily on Mostar in my mind, but we had reports and we knew about the situation. Not only did we read situation reports, there were daily briefings within the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as -- just one example of that and to pick up on a question put to you today by Mr. Praljak at page 46, line 1: "Did a single assistant of yours stay in Mostar for the full 24 hours and with military precision count how many shells landed on the east bank and how many on the west bank and where the shells originated from?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could ask, with the assistance of e-court, if I could have Exhibit P 07255 put on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to tell my learned friend that in addition to quoting question, he should also quote the answer given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. This is not -- this is not required. This is absolutely not required, and it's just to harass me to use the limited time that I have to put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, and this is also for all the Defence counsel, you're not a popular jury here. We are all professionals in this courtroom. We understand the case. We understand this case. We've been working on this case for more than a year. We have the documents in front of us, and we've been listening to the witness here for three days. So when a question is put to the witness, we can correct it if there are some things that are not quite clear. So do not start harassing your colleagues. This might be something that could impress a popular jury, but this will not work with us professional Judges. Of course if the Prosecutor makes a mistake, you can intervene, but let him do his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you have that document in front of you, and this is in fact an UNMO report that the Chamber has previously seen, dated the 19th of December, 1993, just as an example, would you look at -- would you go to F, would you go to section F on page 2 with the usher's assistance, please. In F and number 3 under F -- excuse me, no, I'm sorry. Number 2: "Warring party conflict activity: BiH authorities reported infantry attack by HVO across the confrontation line in the early hours of the morning." Now, in order to save time going to the end of that: "Between 1400 and 1440 hours HVO fired 25 tank rounds into East Mostar." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that an example of the type of a specific example of a report that you would receive about shelling in east Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really believe that this has nothing to do with cross-examination. We were talking about the month of April and the summer of 1993. This is the document dated the 19th of December, 1993. We were referring here to at least 15 different wars with different hallmarks.
