I believe that this report cannot serve as the basis for gauging the number of shells because it dates back to the month of December 1993. We were speaking about the period far earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, the mischaracterisations and the harassment continues. I quoted exactly what General Praljak put to the witness and he challenged this witness: Give me one report, give me one report, where this was reported. And in the 15 minutes of time I had available during the break, I found at least one report where he says 25 tank shells fired by the HVO into East Mostar on that day. That is one example in response to the questions that were put to the witness. I'm giving the witness a chance to respond to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But at a critical point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The Chamber will know what to make of this document and now let the Prosecution do the re-examination. This really gives the impression of a manoeuvre to sabotage. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course the Trial Chamber knows its position, but I do not know what your position will be and that's why I have to draw your attention to the fact that this goes beyond the scope of cross-examination, because Praljak was referring to a different time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No time period was indicated in his questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were also referred by Defence counsel to Defence Exhibit 1D 01543.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can please have that in e-court quickly, please. 1D 01543.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we could go to -- if we could go to the -- excuse me, to this next page, please. Well, in the interests of time, let me just say: This was a document that you were shown by the Defence in connection with this agreement between Izetbegovic and Tudjman from mid-1992 -- or excuse me, in November 1992, as we see on the screen now. Sir, you also -- and I just put that into context -- I point that out for the context of my next question. Despite this letter having been sent by the Croatian representative to the UN on this day, we also looked during your direct examination at Exhibit 75 -- P 00752.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could have that, please. If he has the binder, the binder may be faster. Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you could quickly find Exhibit 752. I think you have it.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this document was issued by the Security Council -- Security Council Resolution 787, just a very few days after the document we were just looking at. As we looked at before, the -- if we go to paragraph number 5 on page 3 of the Resolution, of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Page 5.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Toward the end of that, and I'm going to ask you a couple of questions based on this particular language, starting on the third line from the bottom of page 5: "Including the requirement that all forces, in particular elements of the Croatian army, be withdrawn or be subject to the authority of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or be disbanded or disarmed." Now, my question to you: During this time period, during your period of involvement with the former Yugoslavia, can you tell the Judges any time you're aware of when any element of the Croatian army was put under the command of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know of any time where any Croatian army that was operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina was disbanded or disarmed?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By the way, the previous exhibit that we were looking at, that was shown to you by Defence counsel, at the last paragraph refers to -- that was Exhibit 1D 01543. On the last page of that letter sent by the Croatian representative to the UN that we looked at previously, on the last page of that document it lists Slobodan Praljak as General Major in the Croatian army and Deputy Defence Minister of the Republic of Croatia. Let me just ask you, and also based upon the questions that Mr. Praljak put, did you ever have any dealings with Mr. Praljak during the time that you were involved in these matters?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were asked questions by Defence counsel about Mr. Ganic and others, perhaps Muslim politicians, what term we would like to use, representatives of the BiH government, seeking support, financial and otherwise, in the United States and other international locations. Did you ever have occasion to look at whether Croatian politicians and figures were also doing the same thing?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object. I don't believe we were asking -- we ever indicated financial support. Obviously, Mr. Ganic was, and in fact the Office of the Prosecutor investigated him on that, but that wasn't the gist of our question. We pointed out that Mr. Ganic was seeking political support primarily from the United States in order to engage or to get the United States army involved -- armed forces involved in the conflict. That was the gist. It had nothing to do with financial support, although we do agree that Mr. Ganic was going around the Arab countries and all sorts of other places, establishing -- getting funds in order to break the embargo, purchasing weapons, and so on and so forth. But that wasn't the gist of our question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I would like to join the Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, and my fellow Judge, Judge Trechsel, to ask you and all the Defence counsel really to let the Prosecution finish its redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the questions posed, Your Honour, have to be correct. He cannot misquote me. I never indicated that it was for financial support. It was for political support, and there's a big difference in trying to engage the United States. That was my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, this support, according to the Defence, there was never any talk about any financial support.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas just told us that that is in fact their position, but let me rephrase it because I want to save as much time as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, I put my question to you in the form of -- in particular focused on financial support because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object, because now it goes beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No. Mr. Karnavas just said the scope of cross-examination was political support, so now in response to the objection I'm going to put my question based on political support, which is what Mr. Karnavas just said was his cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I said that I asked before -- I said I'm rephrasing my question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question to you, and that is: Based upon your knowledge and involvement with these issues at the time, is it fair to say that all the parties to the conflict were seeking political support for their positions in the international community?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think that should be a controversial point, but one never knows. You were asked by counsel for, I believe, Mr. Stojic whether Mr. Halilovic made a statement for the media following the meetings on the 19th. I believe it was the second day, the 19th of April, 1993. And again just so the record is balanced, did Mr. -- to your knowledge or information, did Mr. Petkovic and representatives of the Bosnian Croat side also make statements to the media around that time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I answered. I said everybody made statements to the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown a great deal of -- number of orders by a number of Defence counsel, military documents and orders by the ABiH side about possible preparations for military operations. You were sent down to Mostar specifically for the purpose because the international community's assessment at the time was this was about to blow open into open war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it surprise you - would it surprise you - to find documents on both sides, on the HVO and on the ABiH, talking about preparations for military action in that environment?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm putting myself at risk to being criticised by you, but I really believe that this question is not proper. The Prosecutor should say -- should show the witness a document instead of saying, "Would it surprise you," because the Prosecutor is speculating on the HVO in that period of time. The witness might answer, "I wouldn't be surprised," but we haven't seen the documents that are relevant for the question. He should show these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Nozica's comment is on line with what I said myself a long time ago. I believe that I said a long time ago that when you have an order to attack, you will find documents -- if the ABiH is conducting an attack, you will find documents, and if it is the HVO, you will also find documents. It seems to me that it's something I said following a discussion on the 9th of May. We had said that if there had been an attack by the HVO, then there must be documents, because attacks do not happen out of the blue. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question, Your Honour, was, would it surprise the witness in this situation that there would be military orders on both sides making military preparations, and I think that there's no objection to that question. His answer was, "There's no surprise."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should really ask for your ruling on my objection. I believe the question an improper one, calling for speculation. The Prosecutor may first show the witness relevant documents and then put the question on that basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think it's a hypothetical, a hypothetical question. If there should be, would it surprise you. I do not think it is necessary to show such a document, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in addition to that -- thank you, Judge Trechsel. In addition to that, I will appeal to the Chamber's knowledge of all the documents and exhibits that they have seen to date on these matters, and I certainly don't have time in the next four minutes to put them all in front of the witness. Now, can I ask the witness please to be shown in e-court Exhibit P 01804.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as one example, and there's other like it and I'll just say for the record, there's a similar article that is -- I'm not calling it up but at P 01808. Do you recall it being reported and do you recall having information around the time, and I'm directing your attention - if the usher could please scroll down a bit so we can see more of the middle of the page: "The HVO set an April 15th deadline for Bosnian" -- "The HVO set an April 15 deadline for Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic to sign a joint communique ratifying the withdrawals." Now, do you recall there being a deadline set by the HVO around the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you another hypothetical. If Sweden was threatened with attack and someone gave Sweden and said, You have until the 15th of April to take some course of action, would the government of Sweden prepare, take military steps to prepare, in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think -- I think now we're going way beyond what a hypothetical should be in this particular courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe so at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We should stick to the facts of the case. And to the previous question, whether he was aware of it or not is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I agree with that point. It is irrelevant because that's the evidence in the case, was he aware of it or not. But the point of the matter is, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Scott's question was a question of a military nature. Should an army of any kind try to prevent an action that is going to take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let's put it into context. We're in Mostar. The ABiH is asked to remove their headquarters. There's already intelligence information that the ABiH are about to launch an offensive. Obviously, the gentleman wasn't aware of any of these facts. So if you're going to pose a hypothetical, we need to pose it with all the facts and cannot just assume facts or choose and cherry-pick the facts that we find helpful. So if he wants to pose a hypothetical based on all the relevant facts, then I have no problem. I tried to do that yesterday and I was attacked vigorously by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The hypothetical is a very simple one and simply made to make the point and is a very basic one that this general can certainly explain and respond to, and that is simply -- and I used exactly the date from this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If Sweden was threatened with some action by the 15th of April, 1993, would the government and the military forces of Sweden take actions or prepare to deal with such a threat?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I surely hope that we had taken actions long before the threat was presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In a similar fashion, sir, you were asked the question, and this is from -- by Counsel Nozica on page 19 of the transcript today, line 3, whether the 4th Corps of the ABiH would not have been or could not have issued orders without Ganic or Halilovic knowing about and being involved in such orders or plans. Sir, as a military man, again, would the same logic apply to military orders issued by the HVO at a large-scale level, at an operational level, that they would not have or could not have been issued without the knowledge and participation of people such as Stojic, Prlic, and Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to object at this point. There's absolutely -- let me finish first. There's absolutely no evidence, none; in fact, there's plenty of evidence to suggest that Dr. Prlic had nothing to do with military matters. Now, posing that question assumes a fact that's not in evidence. It's basic, it's elementary, and it's improper for the Prosecution to pose a question in that fashion and he knows it. I wasn't here during the morning session and nobody stood up to object to a very objectionable question -- to respond to the objection by the Prosecution. Now I'm here; I am objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's exactly the question --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I also have to object. The Prosecution has already done that once and Mr. Stojic's name was recorded in the transcript. I must say that Mr. Ganic's and Mr. Halilovic's function in no way are comparable to the function and post of Mr. Stojic held at that point in time. The Supreme Command of the HVO was Mr. Boban and not Mr. Stojic. Therefore, bringing the two into connection, Mr. Stojic, with a knowledge of the orders, is absolutely out of order. The Prosecution can ask questions, questions can be answered, but I want to point this out: It is an intentional mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was a question of inference from the documents and it was simply a logical question, and there is no more different basis for the questions that counsel put to him on that point than the foundation that I'm talking about. Simply as matter of military logic. And if the Defence can ask that question on exactly the same basis, then the Prosecution can ask the same question as a matter of military logic and structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The problem is, Your Honour, Izetbegovic is the Commander-in-Chief of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Stojic was the Minister of Defence and Mr. Prlic was the President of the government, and Mr. Petkovic was the head of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, as the President of the government, has nothing to do with the military and the gentleman knows that. Who's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Who is the Supreme Commander? It's Mate Boban. Now, I don't see that name being mentioned. Why? Because Mr. Mate Boban isn't here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will be happy to include him. And Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The point is, unless he can lay a foundation, he cannot just ask a question and assume a fact that's not in evidence. And that's basic. Whether it's continental or whether it's common law, it's basic. And that's why I object to the form of the question. It's an insinuation. He has the burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt that Dr. Prlic had control over the military, and asking hypothetical questions is not a form of proving that. So he can ask it until he's blue. He's got to prove it. And so far, thus far, one year into the case, not one single shred of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's Mr. Karnavas's position which we don't share. But in any event, Your Honour, I think the point is made and I think the Trial Chamber can draw the conclusions that the same logic would apply to both sides. Let me go on because we're already over time, but if I can finish my last question or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The time that you -- when Mr. -- which has much been discussed, the intervention of Mr. Stojic on the meeting of the 18th of April, 1993. In connection with that, and not only that but other parts of the cross-examination, the Defence counsel have put a great deal of emphasis on the last few days on what was happening in Central Bosnia. Let me ask you this, sir: When Mr. Stojic intervened on the 18th of April, 1993, or when you met with him again the following day, on the 19th of April, at the Ministry of Defence, on either occasion when he was talking about Central Bosnia and all the terrible things that were happening, did he ever mention to you the HVO atrocities committed in Ahmici on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is in your report of these -- of your mission, it says that on the 19th of April, when you met with Mr. Stojic, he complained to you about the British Battalion. Now, the British Battalion was based in Central Bosnia, so the complaint presumably was about something that had happened in Central Bosnia involving the British Battalion. Do you recall what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a question about the British Battalion was not a question raised in cross-examination and therefore I consider that the questions being asked now are outside the scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me make the connection, Your Honour. Let me -- allow me to make the connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your report, and I'm looking specifically at the report, it says: "He complained about the behaviour of the British Battalion and I told him to give me all such complaints in writing."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honour, that's not what I asked. I did not ask that. You can put questions like that in an examination-in-chief and I don't know where Mr. Scott is going and I don't know if it's essential or not, but we must respect the rules. His questions can only relate to issues raised during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you want to establish -- what did you want establish talking about Ahmici and the British Battalion, and Ms. Nozica did not address this issue during her cross-examination. She did not discuss the interview between Mr. Stojic and the witness on this particular point, and Ahmici and the British Battalion were not mentioned. What is it you wish to establish?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's quite clear, quite relevant, Your Honour, because the Defence have spent a great deal of time, a number of them, the last two days talking about Central Bosnia and everything that was happening there and how that was, you know, everything that was happening and at then at this particular meeting on the 19th Stojic complains about the British Battalion, something that the British Battalion did in Central Bosnia. So obviously he had something, he had knowledge of Central Bosnia, he was complaining about Central Bosnia, he was complaining about the British Battalion in Central Bosnia, and my question to the witness is in spite of all, that in spite of all that, did he ever mention to you that on the 16th of April the HVO had committed atrocities in Ahmici. So he knew about something the British Battalion had done, but he didn't complain, he didn't complain or acknowledge the fact that these horrendous HVO crimes had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor is now parading in the courtroom and that cannot be allowed. Quite simply, despite my objections and your cautions he is insistent in putting forward his thesis about what he would like to have the meeting described as. However, in the report that the Prosecution is quoting from, there is no mention of Ahmici at all, and this is being construed now. He wishes to leave the impression that certain things happened against the HVO in Bosnia that's the witness acknowledged that he didn't have this information, but once he was shown the documents he accepts that that's how it was. Now, would you please tell the Prosecutor to continue his questioning based on the questions raised in the cross-examination. If he abides by that I won't rise to my feet to object any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the relevance is this Your Honour, the relevance is this: And what happened in Ahmici is a matter of Tribunal adjudicated fact and judgements that have been sustained on appeal. There is no question about that. There is no question about that. The relevance of the question is they've tried to justify Mr. Stojic's outburst and everything he said on the 18th and 19th and in his meetings, and I think the Chamber should be aware of the time that he was protesting these things and raising, not once did he see fit to deal with the issue of Ahmici. Not once. And I must follow a similar question to that and it's quite relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honour, Your Honour, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A lot has gone into the transcript, the record, can I just add that the general should be asked whether Mr. Stojic told the general about the 16 civilians killed in Trusina on the 16th of April 1993. If he's mentioning Ahmici, then just ask him -- may he be asked about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: At this moment in the proceeding the Prosecution can put questions. It's not for the Defence to tell the Prosecution which questions they should ask.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave an example but did not receive a reply. Is it possible for the -- for the Prosecution to ask questions outside the scope of the cross-examination? The Prosecution has now laid the foundations, but did Mr. Stojic speak about the other crimes that took place against the Croats? The crimes were not mentioned by Mr. Stojic at all during that conversation. So in that context may what I had to say be evaluated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... of the question was as follows: You meet Mr. Stojic on the 18th of April. During that period, the question we have to put to you is this one: Did Mr. Stojic discuss with you what might have happened in Central Bosnia or did he not mention anything whatsoever? As you recollect, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only reference to Central Bosnia, as I refer, was his complaint about the British Battalion behaving badly and one other aspect. I don't remember which one for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's in the reports, Your Honour. It's in the ECMM reports that all sides have put in which in Stojic came in, complained about what was happening in Vitez, Novi Travnik, Busovaca. The Chamber has seen all those orders. And it's simply to balance -- it's a fair comment to clarify with this witness that at the same time that Mr. Stojic was launching into a tirade against Mr. Ganic on these points, he did -- he failed to mention the HVO atrocities committed in Ahmici at the same time on the 16th of April, two days before this meeting. And my last question to the witness on this:

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, my final question to you on this point and similar question: At any time during either the 18th or 19th when you were meeting with Mr. Stojic and the other HVO leaders, did any of them mention to you the HVO atrocities committed in Sovici on the 17th of April, the day before?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General, you have now finished your testimony. I'd like to thank you for having come to The Hague to testify. I wish you a safe journey home. Before adjourning for the day, I'd like to turn to Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott, I believe you are going to be calling a witness who will be heard for four days, from what I understood the 92 ter Rule would apply, which would enable Defence teams to have three days for their cross-examination. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that should be the -- Your Honour, just because -- I don't think the time for cross-examination expands to fill the available space. I don't think that's the proper rule, in my respectful submission. We do have a witness scheduled for Monday. We do intend, as much as possible, to present the witness via 92 ter in whole or in part. There may be some viva voce testimony; there may be some from 92 ter and exhibits that we will put to the witness. We're prepared to proceed next week and I think fully prepared. But again, I have to object, Your Honour, if -- the logic of that argument is that the more efficient -- the more efficient and fairly the Prosecution operates, the more time the Defence gets for cross-examination and I object to that rationale. If it's four hours on one side, it can be four hours on the other side, and just because we finish on Monday doesn't mean they get three days or the rest of the week. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, in light of the document which you have prepared, you expected to hear this witness for four days. I'm not saying anything more than that. This is a document which I'd like to show you. I'd like to thank all and everyone. We shall meet again next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of June, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
